docs.abstract: Bags that complement the label’s edgy, yet polished, aesthetic will hit stores this month.
docs.snippet: Bags that complement the label’s edgy, yet polished, aesthetic will hit stores this month.
docs.lead_paragraph: “I always carry my iPhone, keys, credit card and some gloss,” says Nicole Colovos, the co-designer for Helmut Lang. She and her husband, Michael, are gearing up for the first collection of bags to hit the stores since they took over the label in 2006. “We developed all new hardware and looked at bones and bird claws for inspiration and used hints of military finishes,” Michael says. Available this month, the bags come in tough washed creta leather and smooth napa and have a whole lot of zippers. Styles range from duffels and messengers to clutches and pouchettes — just the right complement to their edgy-yet-polished motorcycle-jacket-and-skinny-leather-pants aesthetic. The Syn, a spiraling half-clutch/half-shoulder bag made from Perch skin, blends Michael’s past as a commercial fisherman (straps have fisherman knots and braids) and Nicole’s penchant for utilitarian dressing. “We wanted to create something sculptural, in an interesting fabrication, yet keep it functional,” Nicole says. We couldn’t ask for more. Except maybe a shoe collection. Hint, hint.

headline.main: Helmut Lang’s Got a Brand New Bag

docs.abstract: Coming out of the All-Star break and into the serious part of the regular season, a player-by-player assessment of the Rangers.
docs.snippet: Coming out of the All-Star break and into the serious part of the regular season, a player-by-player assessment of the Rangers.
docs.lead_paragraph: Fifty-two games down, 30 to go, the All-Star break behind us and the final third of the regular season looming ahead. This is the time when the hockey gets serious and you start checking the standings — the right time to look at how the Rangers are doing, man by man. Their official N.H.L. record is 29-20-3, which really means they’re 29-23, but that’s still a quite-good .558 winning percentage. Coach John Tortorella’s team just might be going places, especially now that they’re starting to get their injured forwards back (Ryan Callahan and Vinny Prospal are the first, with Brandon Dubinsky and Eric Christensen soon to follow). Tortorella’s emphasis on conditioning has paid off in strong third-period performances (the Rangers lead the league in comeback wins with seven, two more than anyone else), and he has mellowed somewhat from the volcanic-tempered coach of the previous season.

headline.main: The Rangers at the Top of the Stretch

docs.snippet: “Into Eternity” is Michael Madsen’s documentary about a site being built in Finland to bury nuclear waste for 100,000 years.
docs.lead_paragraph: I am tempted to call “Into Eternity” the most interesting documentary, and one of the most disturbing films, of the year so far, but such a pronouncement, always dubious in early February, seems especially absurd in this case. The film, directed by Michael Madsen — a Danish Conceptual artist, not the American tough-guy actor — takes an unusually long view. Mr. Madsen’s ruminative, even-toned narration is directed not at present-day critics but at viewers who may happen upon this visual artifact at some remote date in the future, as much as 100,000 years from now.

docs.lead_paragraph: Eastern District, the name of this spacious new store, was what they once called the industrial area of Brooklyn encompassing parts of Greenpoint, Bushwick and Williamsburg, said Beth Lewand, who owns the store, along with her husband, Chris Gray. A former Polish butcher shop, it’s lined with shelves and counters that feature about 50 cheeses and many cured meats, mostly American; and sweets including cupcakes from Robicelli’s in Sunset Park in flavors like Creamsicle and almond mocha truffle. They stock about 100 different beers and have a rotating selection on tap for filling growlers. And the shelves are lined with condiments and snacks, mostly bearing Brooklyn labels. They also sell cheese boards from Daskam & Dworkis, furniture makers nearby, who fashion the boards from scrap wood and barter them to Eastern District for cheese.

docs.snippet: Mikuni, a Seattle importer and distributor, ages maple syrup and vinegar in charred-oak barrels used for bourbon.
docs.lead_paragraph: Aging maple syrup in charred-oak barrels used for bourbon has become something of a trend. Mikuni, a Seattle importer and distributor, uses barrels from Tuthilltown Spirits in Gardiner, N.Y., for its Noble Tonic 01, a maple syrup with a subtly spiked edge, and the flask-like bottle is so handsome I would put it on my breakfast table without decanting it into a pitcher. Once the syrup has been bottled, the company uses the same barrels to age 10-year-old Spanish sherry vinegar for another six months for Noble Tonic 03, giving it a more deeply mellow complexity. Noble Tonic 02 is a maple syrup flavored with vanilla and chamomile. They also age French chardonnay vinegar with Egyptian lemon, similar to Meyer lemon, for an added citric touch in their Noble Tonic 04.

docs.snippet: What the high rollers want in a sake is something flagrantly expensive and difficult to find.
docs.lead_paragraph: ERIC SWANSON was on a mission. He needed to track down the sake of the gods. Each time the Lunar New Year rolls around, casinos in Las Vegas begin bracing for an influx of “whales” from Asia — high-rolling gamblers who, when dining and drinking between marathon bouts at the gaming tables, tend to specialize in the grandest of gestures. When they’re eating at the top Japanese restaurants in town, the whales don’t want nice little $20 (or even $200) bottles of sake. The sake should be ambrosial, sure, but what they really want is something flagrantly expensive and difficult to find.

headline.main: In Las Vegas, a Good Story Helps Sell Expensive Sakes

docs.abstract: A private group dedicated to saving the United States, a 1952 ocean liner that has been mothballed in Philadelphia since 1996, announced Tuesday that it had purchased the ship for $3 million.
docs.snippet: A private group dedicated to saving the United States, a 1952 ocean liner that has been mothballed in Philadelphia since 1996, announced Tuesday that it had purchased the ship for $3 million.
docs.lead_paragraph: A private group dedicated to saving the United States, a once-glamorous 1952 ocean liner that has been mothballed in Philadelphia since 1996, announced Tuesday that it had purchased the ship for $3 million. The SS United States Conservancy has been seeking development plans for the rusting hulk, a restoration job that could cost more than $200 million, according to Susan Gibbs, the group’s president. In November, the conservancy proposed making the liner part of a casino project in Philadelphia; competing plans for Miami and New York City are also under discussion. Ms. Gibbs called the New York idea “especially promising” but would not comment further. The group is seeking $1 million in donations to save portions of the ship’s engine rooms, which are largely intact, and for other preservation work. A $5.8 million gift from H. F. Lenfest, a Philadelphia philanthropist, covered the sale price and about 20 months of maintenance.

headline.main: Pennsylvania: Ocean Liner Finds Buyer

docs.abstract: The Senate Ethics Committee named a special counsel to help determine whether to bring formal charges against Senator John Ensign in the circumstances surrounding his cover up of an affair.
docs.snippet: The Senate Ethics Committee named a special counsel to help determine whether to bring formal charges against Senator John Ensign in the circumstances surrounding his cover up of an affair.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Senate Ethics Committee announced Tuesday that it has named a special counsel to help determine whether to bring formal charges against Senator John Ensign, the Nevada Republican who has been accused of using his political influence to help cover up an affair he had with the wife of a former top aide. Carol Elder Brown, a former Justice Department prosecutor and an experienced criminal defense lawyer, was appointed to the unusual role, according to a statement released by the committee. She will help with what the committee said is a “preliminary inquiry,” which follows an investigation by staff members that has already taken about a year. Mr. Ensign, who is up for re-election in 2012, has been cleared by investigators at the Department of Justice and the Federal Election Commission.

docs.lead_paragraph: As Europe continues to ship off its up-and-coming actors to play dashing American superheroes, the United States is apparently responding by sending one of its most virile specimens of manhood to that continent in exchange: namely, Woody Allen. Mr. Allen’s latest film, “Midnight in Paris,” will open the Cannes Film Festival on May 11, the event’s organizers said on Wednesday. The film, the 41st feature-length work that Mr. Allen has directed, is a romantic comedy whose cast includes Owen Wilson, Rachel McAdams, Marion Cotillard, Kathy Bates and Adrien Brody, though one cast member, Carla Bruni-Sarkozy, has received a bit more attention than the others. In a statement, Thierry Frémaux, the director of the Cannes festival, described “Midnight in Paris” as “a wonderful love letter to Paris,” adding: “It’s a film in which Woody Allen takes a deeper look at the issues raised in his last films: our relationship with history, art, pleasure and life.” The film will be released in France on the same day it makes its debut at Cannes, though an American release date has not yet been announced. The full Cannes Film Festival runs through May 22.

headline.main: Woody Allen’s ‘Midnight in Paris’ Will Open Cannes Festival

docs.abstract: The company’s new piece, “Five Blind Mice,” as seen at the Irondale Center in Fort Greene, Brooklyn, is a tour de force of choreography and technology.
docs.snippet: The company’s new piece, “Five Blind Mice,” as seen at the Irondale Center in Fort Greene, Brooklyn, is a tour de force of choreography and technology.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Adam Scher Dance Company’s new piece, “Five Blind Mice,” which was presented last week at the Irondale Center in Fort Greene, Brooklyn, is a tour de force of choreography and technology. Kate Atherton, Molly Merkler, Veronica Carnero, Casey Loomis and Adam Scher performed separate vignettes, each specifically programmed by the technical director, Christopher Langer, to sync with the piece’s emotional core. As an opener, Merkler performed in almost complete darkness; a sensor strapped to her stomach detected her breathing and illuminated a light bulb overhead with every inhale. Later in the lineup, Atherton began her more up-tempo piece against the backdrop of a blank projection. As the piece went on, time-lapsed footage of her movements appeared in repetition every 30 seconds, creating an army of her own image that seemingly danced along with the real performer.

headline.main: Notes From the Underground | Adam Scher Dance Company

docs.lead_paragraph: A quick thought about the Egyptian uprising. Many people have sought parallels either in the Philippines 1986 or in Indonesia 1998; I’ve done it myself. But there is a possibly important or revealing difference. As the chart above shows, both of those political crises followed on drastic economic crises — Marcos was caught up in the Latin American debt crisis of the 1980s (in some important ways the Philippines was in effect a Latin American economy at the time), Suharto in the Asian financial crisis. Nothing comparable for Egypt now.

docs.lead_paragraph: David Brooks: Gail, every few years we turn on the TV and we see the main square of some foreign capital filled with people and before too long, a dictator falls. This is truly a great time to be alive. Now, I understand all the worries that go along with this. I understand my Israeli friends who feel that they are in the process of losing the least bad Egyptian leader. But my bottom line is this: the world will be far safer when more of the world is normal, meaning mostly open and mostly democratic. If we have to go through a period of turmoil to get there, it is more than worth it. That’s especially true in the Middle East.

docs.lead_paragraph: ‘This is Not God’s Work’ Bill Gross: “Fifty years ago, the highest paid and most prestigious professions were that of a doctor or a 707 airline pilot who flew the “golden” route from Los Angeles to Honolulu. Today the yellow brick road begins on Wall Street or the City. Aside from supernova innovators such as Steve Jobs or Mark Zuckerberg, the money is made from securitizing things instead of booting and rebuilding America. . .. Almost a quarter of the 400 wealthiest people on Forbes annual richest list make their money from money, whereas only 8% could make that claim in its first issue in 1982, and probably close to 0% when I first read my economic primer in 1966. docs.lead_paragraph: THERE was a time when only beggars went bareheaded. This was some while ago, a century or so. But up until World War II and the period just after, a gentleman was not considered properly dressed without a hat. Even the names of hats were rich in character and historical association. The bowler, or derby, with the rigid shape of an upended bean pot, was named for a 19th-century English earl who popularized the style. The fedora’s name came from a play of that title, written for Sarah Bernhardt by the otherwise largely forgotten French dramatist Victorien Sardou.

docs.lead_paragraph: The musician who first took the stage of the Apollo Theater in Harlem as Little Stevie Wonder at age 12 in 1962 and then went on to some very big things will receive an  honor from the theater later this year. The Apollo is to announce on Wednesday that it will induct Mr. Wonder – he’s just Stevie now, thank you very much – into its Apollo Legends Hall of Fame. Mr. Wonder, the best-selling pop and soul artist whose albums include “Talking Book,” “Innervisions” and “Songs in the Key of Life,” was a child performer on Berry Gordy’s Motown Revue when he made his Apollo debut, and returned several times to the theater for performances including its “Save the Apollo” concert in the 1980s and a series of solo shows in 2005, the theater’s press representatives said. Other artists already named to the theater’s Hall of Fame include Michael Jackson, Aretha Franklin, Quincy Jones, Smokey Robinson and Ella Fitzgerald. Mr. Wonder is to be officially inducted on June 13 at the Apollo’s annual spring gala.

headline.main: Stevie Wonder to Be Named to Apollo Theater’s Hall of Fame

docs.abstract: A recipe for four.
docs.snippet: A recipe for four.
docs.lead_paragraph: 2 tablespoons unsalted butter 1 small yellow onion, peeled and diced small 2 cloves garlic, peeled and minced 2 cups white rice 1 tablespoon thyme leaves 1 13-ounce can coconut milk 1 Scotch bonnet pepper, whole (optional) 1 cup cooked pigeon peas 2 tablespoons chopped scallion, green part only Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste 1. Melt butter in a medium sauce pan set over low heat. When it begins to foam, add the onion and the garlic, stir, and allow these to soften in the heat, about 3 minutes. 2. Add the rice and the thyme, and stir to combine. Add the coconut milk and 2 ½ cups water, and turn heat to high. Bring liquid to a simmer, then lower heat. If using pepper, place it in center of pot. Cover. Cook until the liquid is absorbed and rice is soft, approximately 25 minutes. Remove from heat and fluff with a fork. If using pepper, remove it. Add peas and scallions, then stir to combine. Season to taste with salt and pepper, then cover pot again and keep warm until ready to serve. Serves 4.

headline.main: Coconut-Scented Rice

docs.lead_paragraph: “Kahn in Venice,” an exhibition at the Italian Cultural Institute in Los Angeles, celebrates the architect Louis I. Kahn’s special relationship with Italy. His unbuilt 1968 project for a congress hall in Venice is the centerpiece of the show, which was organized in collaboration with the Architectural Archives of the University of Pennsylvania, and which also includes many of Kahn’s lush, expressive travel sketches of buildings, gardens, bridges and street scenes in Venice, Rome and the hill towns of Tuscany. (The exhibition, which is on view through March 19, was curated and designed by the Los Angeles architects Barton Myers and David Karp, both of whom were Kahn’s students and apprentices.)

docs.lead_paragraph: In our column today, the Bagger looks at the documentary race, where there may actually be some drama. Not that you would know it from the behavior of the presumed front-runner, Charles Ferguson, the director of “Inside Job,” his dissection of the financial meltdown. Mr. Ferguson, an early Internet millionaire, is soft-spoken and unconcerned with appearances; he’s been known to show up at awards shows in sneakers. He’s been through the Oscar process before, with his first film, “No End in Sight,” in 2008. What’s changed in his approach since then? “I have an agent now, which I never did before,” he said. “I’ve spoken to the Sony publicity people a few times.” (Sony Pictures Classics is the distributor of “Inside Job,” which is being re-released in theaters on the back of its Oscar nomination.) “But,” he added of the Oscar race, “this is totally not my department.”

docs.abstract: With only one season under her belt, Giovanna Randall, the designer behind the New York-based label Honor, is opening a shop in the meatpacking district.
docs.snippet: With only one season under her belt, Giovanna Randall, the designer behind the New York-based label Honor, is opening a shop in the meatpacking district.
docs.lead_paragraph: With only one season under her belt, Giovanna Randall, the designer behind the New York-based label Honor, is opening a shop in the meatpacking district. But there is more in store than Randall’s girlie cocktail dresses and long chiffon evening gowns. Like the label that shares its name, Honor is all about the prettier, finer points of a woman’s pleasures. “I started asking myself, ‘What do you think Sophia Loren’s couch looks like?’ or ‘What kind of typewriter would Grace Kelly have used?’ ” the designer says. Randall plans to display her collection alongside vintage and new books. Cafe treats like Bellocq tea and espresso are a small step toward Randall’s dream of turning Honor into a multidimensional lifestyle brand. “I fantasize about coming by the shop and being able to pick up a lovely party dress and wonderful bouquet of flowers en route to a friend’s birthday dinner.” So do we.

headline.main: Now Opening | Honor

docs.abstract: With the death last month of Daniel Bell, we lost a prescient big thinker on many subjects, including ideology and American politics.
docs.snippet: With the death last month of Daniel Bell, we lost a prescient big thinker on many subjects, including ideology and American politics.
docs.lead_paragraph: With the death last month of Daniel Bell, America lost its last great 20th-century big thinker, though this is not necessarily the impression many now have of him. One reason is that Bell was most prolific during a period, 1950-80, bounded by the cold war, that has receded into the half-forgotten past. Another is that for most of his career, Bell was seen less as a singular figure than as one of a club of intellectuals whose pedigrees were so similar they seemed interchangeable — New York City-reared Jews trained in factional combat at City College and groomed as journalists in the pages of small-circulation magazines (The New Leader, Commentary, Partisan Review, Encounter, The Public Interest), with detours into the Luce empire (Bell was for a time the labor editor of Fortune) and university perches (in Bell’s case Columbia and Harvard).

headline.main: Daniel Bell, Master Builder

docs.abstract: Despite setbacks, the capital of Chile is alive with innovation that stretches from fashion to art to food and beyond.
docs.snippet: Despite setbacks, the capital of Chile is alive with innovation that stretches from fashion to art to food and beyond.
docs.lead_paragraph: LIKE the on-again, off-again construction of the city’s Costanera Center, which will include South America’s tallest skyscraper, Santiago is reaching for the skies while progress moves forward in fits and starts, thanks in part to natural disasters like the 8.8 magnitude quake that rocked the country last year. Still, there’s a spirit of enterprise in the capital, which was the top destination in the New York Times Travel section’s “The 41 Places to Go in 2011” feature. From a growing fashion movement to government initiatives to create a Silicon Valley of the South, there is an energy that just can’t be suppressed. Long gone are the days when the city was derided for its food scene or seen as sleepy and staid. Arts sites like the Centro Gabriela Mistral, which opened in September, along with cutting-edge galleries, boutiques and stand-out restaurants, attest to an urban scene that has blossomed in the wake of a repressive dictatorship now long dead.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Santiago, Chile

docs.abstract: He’s been nominated for an Oscar nine times, starting with “The Shawshank Redemption” in 1994, and never won. He’s on deck again this year, for the Coen brothers’ “True Grit.”
docs.snippet: He’s been nominated for an Oscar nine times, starting with “The Shawshank Redemption” in 1994, and never won. He’s on deck again this year, for the Coen brothers’ “True Grit.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Roger Deakins is almost the Susan Lucci of cinematography: he’s been nominated for an Oscar nine times, starting with “The Shawshank Redemption” in 1994, and never won. He’s on deck again this year, for the Coen brothers’ “True Grit.” Many of his honors came from his collaboration with the Coens; he has been their go-to cinematographer since “Barton Fink.” They first met more than two decades ago, at a coffee shop in Notting Hill, in London. “By then they were great cult filmmakers,” Mr. Deakins said, in a phone interview from his home in Santa Monica. “I don’t know why they had chosen to meet with me, but they did and we got on.” Does he understand them any better now? “I guess,” he said, laughing. But Mr. Deakins professed as much surprise as the Coens have about “True Grit” being such a box office hit. “It’s maybe more accessible than most of their films,” he said. “I think it’s a great movie, but I think most of their films are great movies.” He is currently working on “Now,” a futuristic thriller from the director Andrew Niccol (“Gattaca”), his first experience shooting in digital. What does he make of the divide between film and digital? “I don’t really see the point of the argument,” Mr. Deakins said. “You use images and light and texture and camera movement to tell a story. I think it’s a technical argument, and films aren’t really made by technique.”

headline.main: Roger Deakins, the Susan Lucci of Cinematography

docs.snippet: The camera is never really neutral, but in “Staging Action,” an exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art, it’s a co-conspirator.
docs.lead_paragraph: During the last year the Museum of Modern Art has reinvented itself as a Museum of Performance Art. NBC was third for the night, averaging 7.7 million viewers from 8 to 10 for a two-hour edition of “Minute to Win It.” ABC finished in fourth place with reruns for much of prime time before a new episode of “Cougar Town” at 9:30 (6.6 million).

docs.abstract: “The occasional tensions in the foreign policies of the United States and Turkey are a normal stapleof international relations.”
docs.snippet: “The occasional tensions in the foreign policies of the United States and Turkey are a normal stapleof international relations.”
docs.lead_paragraph: The occasional tensions in the foreign policies of the United States and Turkey are a normal staple of international relations. James Traub’s article, though, betrays the arrogance and presumed omniscience of an American “empire,” which expects every nation to be its apostle, i.e., all nations are equal, but some are more equal than others. That approach neither reflects today’s realities, nor would it serve our nation’s interests. The United States, more so than ever, needs countries like Turkey that are willing to pay their fair share and take initiative and responsibility to create a more stable and peaceful world. Turkey today has the resources as well as the will to be such a partner for the United States. Rather than making light of or dismissing Turkey’s well-meaning initiatives to solve conflicts in its neighborhood, our leaders would be well advised to listen more often and more closely to the sage advice of this country. It is this kind of experienced guidance from a friend and an ally, which has existed in that part of the world for a thousand years and ruled it for most of that time, that may well save American blood and treasure in the years ahead.

headline.main: Letter: Turkey’s Rules
headline.print_headline: Turkey’s Rules

docs.lead_paragraph: Rebecca Traister’s thesis in “Cowgirl Country” lacksthe critical consideration that our political scene needs. Except for personal experience with guns, Gabrielle Giffords and Sarah Palin share few specific, substantive biographical details or political ideas. The “cowgirl” identity can’t explain the political impact of Margaret Chase Smith, Shirley Chisholm, Bella Abzug or Elizabeth Holtzman. To reduce the force of women during the American Revolution and the early republic to a “querulous Abigail Adams” does a disservice to a long list of American women and slanders one of our great American voices. To seek “cowgirls” means you won’t find women like Susan B. Anthony, Jane Addams or Margaret Sanger. To reduce Hillary Rodham Clinton’s political appeal to one metaphor ignores the strength of her following.

docs.abstract: The vast winter storm that left its icy mark on much of the nation has moved out. But before the evidence melts, here’s a look back.

docs.lead_paragraph: The vast winter storm that left its icy mark on much of the nation has finally moved offshore. But before many people could even shovel out their cars, a cold snap moved in. The snowy, icy roads may have played a role in a deadly accident near Miami, Okla., where three people died after their pickup truck went off a highway bridge into the Spring River, more than 50 feet below. Several other passengers were rescued from the frigid water. Farther south, another storm threatened to bring more snow, sleet and ice to places that don’t usually see much, from Houston, which canceled school on Friday, through Louisiana and Mississippi. But before the evidence melts, here is a look back.

docs.lead_paragraph: UNDERSTANDABLY, composers through the centuries have responded to the text of the Roman Catholic Requiem and its evocations of the day of wrath, the last trumpet and other apocalyptic images with music of high drama (Mozart) if not overt theatricality (Verdi). docs.lead_paragraph: I remember walking to the post office in the little town where I grew up. Some summer days, there wasn’t much else to do. The postmaster was a remote and taciturn fellow known to me mostly as a blurry hand rifling envelopes into the boxes. This was the early 1970s, and each trip to the building with the flag outside and the “Wanted” posters in the lobby filled me with a sense of possibility. I might discover I won a sweepstakes. I might receive an issue of one of the magazines that I subscribed to chiefly so I would get mail. And even if my family’s box was empty that day, I might overhear a bit of adult gossip or bump into a pal. I might recognize on a poster the scowling face of a man I’d seen hanging around the hardware store, making me eligible for a big reward.

She flirts with him, ­kisses him first, talks back when he tells her off, stays when he buys her a ticket to go. He puts up a fight with all the grim resolve of a guy closing the shutters on a storm that’s about to raze his house. Sooner or later, the dame, who happens to be beautiful, wears him down and he comes around, against his better judgment. docs.lead_paragraph: Vladimir Nabokov claimed that the “initial shiver of inspiration” for “Lolita” came from a newspaper account of an ape in the Jardin des Plantes in Paris that produced the first drawing ever made by an animal. “This sketch,” he reported, “showed the bars of the poor creature’s cage.” The story neatly encapsulates the tragedy and comedy of Humbert Humbert: for all his preternatural brilliance — no one of his kind has ever set such things down on a page — he knows less than nothing because he doesn’t know that a world exists outside himself. The narrator of Benjamin Hale’s first novel, “The Evolution of Bruno Littlemore,” has some of Humbert’s erudition and much of his arrogance. Like Humbert, he is imprisoned for a murder he can’t bring himself to regret, and like Humbert’s, his confession is far less concerned with that act than with the scandalous love affair that precipitated it. The difference is that Bruno knows he is trapped, for he has “seen this cage from both within and without.” Also, Bruno is an actual ape.

docs.lead_paragraph: Cassandra Brooks, the narrator of Bradford Morrow’s new novel, “The Diviner’s Tale,” sees too much, thinks too much and feels too much. And in the telling of her strange tale she also, sadly, talks too much. She is a woman who is visited with unwanted visions, whether of the past or the future or some alternative present she often can’t tell. The novel begins with her account of the very first of what she calls her “forevisions”: when she was 7, she warned her older brother not to go out one summer night, and he was killed in a car crash. In the story’s present tense, she is in her mid-30s, living with her 11-year-old twin sons in the upstate New York town where she was raised, and occasionally turning her paranormal gifts to modest advantage by hiring herself out as a diviner; when asked, she’ll dowse for water in her neighbors’ fields. In the course of one of these expeditions, she sees something terrible — a young girl hanged from a tree. But when she brings the police back to the scene, the body has disappeared without a trace, as if she had simply dreamed it.

docs.lead_paragraph: Unlike the majority of fashion labels, which are subject to a constant wax-and-wane credibility cycle, A.P.C. is ever cool. That’s due in large part to the brand’s founder, Jean Touitou, a man to whom the conventions of fashion — trend-based collections, high-profile ad campaigns — are so many canards, a conviction that his loyal customers, many of whom wouldn’t wear any other jeans, wholeheartedly endorse. A.P.C.’s second Manhattan shop will open next week at the corner of Perry and Bleecker Streets in the West Village, to be followed this summer by a third location just a few blocks away. “The West Village is classy. SoHo is getting a bit commercial. Every time you turn around, there’s a new store. Of course, who am I to talk? I’m opening new stores.” Touitou said with typical candor when The Moment rang up his Paris office to chat. Here, he talks to us about the fashion habits of 19th-century British aristocrats, the pleasures of sewing and why the classics aren’t as simple as they look.

headline.main: Special Delivery | A.P.C.’s New Digs

docs.abstract: A student production of “Joe Turner’s Come and Gone” that overcame the objections of a school superintendent in order to proceed has been temporarily halted by Mother Nature.
docs.snippet: A student production of “Joe Turner’s Come and Gone” that overcame the objections of a school superintendent in order to proceed has been temporarily halted by Mother Nature.
docs.lead_paragraph: A student production of “Joe Turner’s Come and Gone” that overcame the objections of a school superintendent in order to proceed has been temporarily halted by Mother Nature. The Waterbury Arts Magnet School in Waterbury, Conn., had planned to perform that August Wilson play this week, but postponed the performances after the recent heavy snowfalls in the Northeast. Dana Manning, the school’s fine arts coordinator, told The Republican-American newspaper of Waterbury that the bad weather had prevented rehearsals. Additional performances planned for next week were also likely to be rescheduled and new dates were not immediately announced. The Waterbury Board of Education said in January that the school’s production of the play, set in 1911 at a Pittsburgh boardinghouse where several freed slaves reside, could proceed, overruling an earlier decision by the superintendent, David L. Snead. Mr. Snead, who is black, had sought to cancel the play because the word “nigger” appears multiple times in its dialogue. During the board meeting at which the decision was announced, the production was defended by the high school students in its cast, as well as by James Bundy, artistic director of Yale Repertory Theater, where “Joe Turner” and other Wilson plays were developed.

headline.main: School Production Of Wilson Play Delayed

docs.lead_paragraph: A Chinese official, Xu Zhitao, has denied accusations by Indian officials that a revered Tibetan leader living in India is a spy for the Chinese government, Chinese news reports said this week. Indian officials first accused the Tibetan, the 17th Karmapa Lama, left, of being a spy after Indian police officers seized $1.5 million worth of foreign currency, including Chinese renminbi, last month from the lama’s home in Dharamsala. There is a dispute over the Karmapa Lama; a rival candidate who has close ties to Indian intelligence officials claims he is the true lama. Tibetan Buddhism’s spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, backs the one in Dharamsala, seen by many Tibetans as a possible future leader.

Having announced after Cunningham’s death in 2009 that it would give its final performances on New Year’s Eve 2011 in New York, it is saying goodbye to cities and to dances. docs.snippet: The family of Kate McGarrigle, the Canadian singer and songwriter who died last year, has announced two tribute concerts in her honor.
docs.lead_paragraph: The family of Kate McGarrigle, the Canadian singer and songwriter who died last year, has announced two tribute concerts in her honor. Her children, Rufus Wainwright and Martha Wainwright, and McGarrigle’s sister and longtime musical partner, Anna McGarrigle, are scheduled to perform on May 12 and 13 at Town Hall in Manhattan. They will be joined by their third sister, Jane McGarrigle, as well as by Jimmy Fallon, Emmylou Harris, Antony Hegarty, Justin Bond and several other performers, including Michel Pepin on guitar, Chaim Tannenbaum on mandolin and banjo, and Joel Zifkin on violin, all of whom were regular members of the McGarrigle band. “Everyone who met my mother, no matter how briefly, was struck by her worldly character matched with an otherworldly artistic aura,” Mr. Wainwright said of the tribute in an e-mail. “It’s all in the songs now. I can’t wait to hear them performed by all of these incredible artists.” Ms. McGarrigle learned she had a rare form of cancer in 2006 and died at her home in Montreal in January 2010. She was 63. All proceeds from the shows will go toward the creation of the Kate McGarrigle Sarcoma Research Fund, in association with the Sarcoma Foundation of America. Tickets go on sale at noon on Monday: (800) 745-3000; ticketmaster.com.

headline.main: Kate McGarrigle Tributes

docs.lead_paragraph: Movie audiences in North America spent about $75.4 million on tickets over the weekend, a 24 percent decline from a year earlier. The soft result extends Hollywood’s losing streak to 13 “down” weekends in a row. “Avatar,” which was still raking in box office cash at this time last year, is only part of the explanation. A ho-hum batch of releases in recent weeks has also contributed to lackluster sales. For the weekend, a traditionally slow one because of the Super Bowl, “The Roommate” (above, with Minka Kelly, left, and Leighton Meester), a horror entry from Sony Pictures Entertainment, was No. 1 with an estimated $15.6 million, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles box office statistics. “Sanctum,” a 3-D horror film set in underwater caves, was second, selling about $9.2 million for Universal Pictures and Relativity Media. The romantic comedy “No Strings Attached” (Paramount Pictures) was third with about $8.4 million for a new total of $51.8 million. “The King’s Speech” (the Weinstein Company) was a close fourth with roughly $8.3 million ($84.1 million total). “The Green Hornet” (Sony) chugged away in fifth place with $6.1 million, lifting its total to $87.2 million.

headline.main: A Sleepy Winter Continues at the Box Office

docs.lead_paragraph: Not that long ago, the possibility of finding planets outside our solar system was merely theoretical. In 1995, astronomers began to be able to detect Jupiter-sized “exoplanets” by their gravitational effect on the stars they orbit. And with the launch of the Kepler satellite in March 2009 and the release last week of the data it has so far gathered, astronomy has crossed a major threshold. The Kepler has discovered 1,235 potential planets.

docs.lead_paragraph: On the campaign trail in 2008, Barack Obama played to two very different foreign policy constituencies. Often he presented himself as the tribune of the anti-war left  the only candidate who had opposed the invasion of Iraq from the beginning, the man who could be trusted to civilize the global war on terror, and the perfect figure to smooth the transition to a post-American world order. To more bipartisan audiences, though, he cast himself as a cold-eyed realist  the rightful heir to George H. W. Bush, if not Henry Kissinger, who would pursue America’s interests without pretending (as the younger President Bush often did) that they matched up perfectly with America’s democratic ideals.

docs.abstract: America’s role in the peace process.
docs.snippet: America’s role in the peace process.
docs.lead_paragraph: By late last year, the Middle East peace process had become a process in name only. The Obama administration’s hopes of brokering talks between Israel and the Palestinians collapsed after the Israelis dug in their heels over the Palestinian demand for a freeze in settlement construction, a demand backed by Washington. And neither side showed much enthusiasm for the indirect talks mediated by George Mitchell, the State Department envoy to the region. This was the dismal state of play when the Arab world was jolted by an eruption of “people power” in Tunisia, Egypt and elsewhere. Is it possible that these electrodes can shock some life into the inert peace process?

headline.main: The White House Waits
headline.print_headline: The White House Waits

docs.lead_paragraph: The street demonstrations roiling the Arab world have riveted and moved many Americans, who have visions of democracy sweeping through northern Africa and the Middle East. As I write this, Hosni Mubarak, Egypt’s president, has announced he will not stand for re-election, as has Yemen’s longtime ruler, Ali Abdullah Saleh. Tunisia’s ruler fled, and the nation has a new government; King Abdullah of Jordan replaced his own cabinet and now has a prime minister who promises reform. There are even stirrings in Syria. President Obama has signaled his determination to support democratization in the region, as promised in his 2009 Cairo speech, and not to remain tied to authoritarian regimes.

headline.main: A Plan for Peace That Still Could Be

docs.abstract: The thinker Daniel Bell, who died last week, could be impatient with those he judged to be on the wrong side of history or ideas, as is clear from his correspondence with William F. Buckley Jr. in 1955.
docs.snippet: The thinker Daniel Bell, who died last week, could be impatient with those he judged to be on the wrong side of history or ideas, as is clear from his correspondence with William F. Buckley Jr. in 1955.
docs.lead_paragraph: Daniel Bell, who died last week at 91, is closely associated with a group of New York intellectuals who included Irving Kristol, Nathan Glazer and Daniel Patrick Moynihan. But as I write in an essay for the Feb. 13 Book Review (published early online), Bell deserves our attention as a singular — and singularly ambitious — thinker and writer, who followed in the system-building tradition of Karl Marx and Thorstein Veblen, both heroes of his. Like them, Bell could be impatient with those he judged to be on the wrong side of history or ideas, even in those post-war years remembered for their cozy political “consensus,” as is clear from Bell’s correspondence with William F. Buckley Jr. in 1955.

headline.main: Two Anti-Communists at Odds

docs.snippet: Mr. Moore on Monday filed suit against Bob and Harvey Weinstein, who through their specially formed Fellowship Adventure Group distributed “Fahrenheit 9/11” in an alliance with Lionsgate and IFC Films, claiming that the Weinsteins defrauded him.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Fahrenheit 9/11,” Michael Moore’s 2004 documentary about President George W. Bush, is still generating heat. Mr. Moore on Monday filed suit against Bob and Harvey Weinstein, who formed Fellowship Adventure Group to distribute “Fahrenheit 9/11” in an alliance with Lionsgate and IFC Films, claiming that the Weinsteins defrauded him of at least $2.7 million in profits from the film. The suit, filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court, charged the Weinsteins with “accounting tricks and financial deception” in connection with “Fahenheit 9/11,” which took in about $222 million at the worldwide box office, and millions more on home video. Bert Fields, a lawyer for the Weinsteins, said Mr. Moore had been paid everything he was due, and was trying to make a public spectacle out of what he called “a routine kind of auditing” dispute. “Mr. Moore has put in a number of very inflammatory claims designed for the press,” Mr. Fields added. “He should be ashamed of himself.” Larry Stein, a lawyer for Mr. Moore, said in a statement that Mr. Moore had never sued anyone in his filmmaking career and that “it’s very sad that it had to come to this.”Mr. Moore and the Weinsteins have worked together on several films, including “Sicko” and “The Big One.”

headline.main: Michael Moore Sues Weinsteins Over ‘Fahrenheit 9/11’

docs.lead_paragraph: A football- and zombie-theme episode of “Glee,” featuring a guest appearance by Katie Couric and a musical mash-up of Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” and the Yeah Yeah Yeahs’ “Heads Will Roll,” received a big boost in the ratings on Sunday from its time slot following the Super Bowl. According to Nielsen’s estimates, Fox’s “Glee” attracted 26.8 million viewers, a record for this hit musical comedy and more than any other scripted series on television in three years. In comparison, however, ratings for the episode fell short of those for last year’s occupant of that highly desirable time slot, CBS’s reality show “Undercover Boss,” which garnered 38.7 million viewers. Final audience figures for “Glee” and Fox’s Super Bowl coverage were not immediately available on Monday; however, Nielsen’s preliminary overnight estimates from the major media markets were up about 3 percent from a year ago, when CBS’s Super Bowl broadcast set a ratings record with 106.5 million viewers, the largest television audience in United States history. Opposite the ratings juggernaut on Fox, CBS fared the best with 3.9 million viewers for a rerun edition of “60 Minutes” at 7, followed by reruns the rest of the night. ABC was third, averaging 2.7 million viewers for the 2007 movie “Knocked Up,” while NBC finished fourth.

headline.main: New High Note for ‘Glee’

docs.lead_paragraph: Representative Al Green, a Houston Democrat, on Monday asked the Justice Department to begin a civil rights investigation after a videotape surfaced that shows Houston police officers beating and kicking a 15-year-old burglary suspect last March as he lay on the ground. Four officers are awaiting trial on misdemeanor charges of official repression in the case, but prosecutors had blocked release of the tape, arguing that it would taint a trial. An ABC television affiliate, KTRK, obtained a copy and broadcast it on Wednesday, reigniting anger over the arrest. On the video, the teenager appears to be clipped by a police car during a chase. He falls, flips onto his stomach and puts his hands behind his head. Several officers rush in, punching and kicking him as they arrest him. “We are outraged at what occurred,” Mr. Green said. The teenager, Chad Holley, was later sentenced to probation for burglary.

This does not mean that political agendas can’t be the subject of academic work — one should inquire into their structure, history, etc. — but that the point of introducing them into the classroom should never be to urge them or to warn against them. I have never felt that my attempts to explain this point have been entirely successful, but I am moved to try again by the recent experience of a conference that, I believe, exemplifies the point in action.

docs.abstract: With a dozen Oscar nominations for “The King’s Speech” and a lengthy profile in Vanity Fair, Harvey Weinstein is thought to be back. But Michael Moore is spoiling the party.
docs.snippet: With a dozen Oscar nominations for “The King’s Speech” and a lengthy profile in Vanity Fair, Harvey Weinstein is thought to be back. But Michael Moore is spoiling the party.
docs.lead_paragraph: He was a high-flying, sometimes-vilified character and he was hanging by a thread – no, we don’t mean Spider-Man. We mean, of course, Harvey Weinstein, the other entertainment behemoth we love to puncture, and caricature. With a dozen Oscar nominations for “The King’s Speech” and a few others scattered elsewhere, Mr. Weinstein is officially back, a turn of events proclaimed by our own David Carr, and solidified twice over, by a lengthy new profile in Vanity Fair, and by a lawsuit. As our colleague Michael Cieply reports, Michael Moore filed suit in Los Angeles against the Weinstein brothers, Harvey and Bob, over profits from “Fahrenheit 9/11,” alleging “accounting tricks and financial deception” that defrauded him of at least $2.7 million in profits from his blockbuster 2004 documentary (or docbuster, as his acolyte Morgan Spurlock calls them).

headline.main: A Lawsuit to Welcome Harvey Weinstein Back

docs.lead_paragraph: The doctor is out, temporarily, and headed back to Broadway: Robert Sean Leonard, who plays the infinitely patient oncologist Dr. James Wilson on the hit Fox medical drama “House,” will return to the stage in the coming revival of “Born Yesterday,” its press representatives said on Tuesday. Mr. Leonard is set to join the production as Paul Verrall, the journalist tasked with educating Billie Dawn, the showgirl and gal pal of the crooked mogul Harry Brock. This latest revival of the Garson Kanin play, which is to begin previews at the Cort Theater on March 31 and open on April 24, previously announced that it would  star Jim Belushi (of “According to Jim”) as Brock and Nina Arianda (“Venus in Fur”) as Dawn, and would be directed by Doug Hughes (“Doubt”). The original 1946 Broadway production starred Paul Douglas, Judy Holliday and Gary Merrill, and the 1950 film version starred Broderick Crawford, Ms. Holliday and William Holden.

docs.lead_paragraph: Based on recent episodes of  “Glee” and the ever-changing loyalties of its characters (not to mention their ever-intertwining love lives), we have absolutely no idea where this hit Fox musical-comedy is headed in the weeks to come. But we know where the cast members will be in May and June: they’ll be hitting the road for another tour of North American arenas and performance spaces. On Tuesday Fox said that a 16-city “Glee Live! in Concert” series will begin on May 21 at the Mandalay Bay Events Center in Las Vegas and conclude on June 18 at the Nassau Coliseum in Uniondale, N.Y. (Another performance in the New York area will be on June 16 at the Izod Center in East Rutherford, N.J.; interestingly, no performance has been scheduled on June 12, the date that the Tony Awards are presented.) A statement from Fox said that the show, conceived by the “Glee” co-creator Ryan Murphy, will feature songs performed on the series, including “Empire State of Mind,” “Toxic,” “It’s My Life” and – deal with it – “Don’t Stop Believin’.”

headline.main: Don’t Stop Believin’ (or Tourin’): ‘Glee’ Cast Hitting the Road Again

docs.lead_paragraph: The elements behind the success of “The Social Network,” as its makers rarely tire of telling us, were an odd mix. There were no stars, save for a pop singer; a subject that was an Internet punch line even before the Internet heard its actual punch lines; directed by a visual mastermind, David Fincher, and based on the pulsing dialogue of Aaron Sorkin – both of them big personalities with opposing styles. Mr. Fincher has been nominated for an Oscar and Mr. Sorkin has already been rewarded; he just won the Writers Guild of America award for best adapted screenplay and is likely to pick up the Oscar in that category as well. At the Writers Guild ceremony in Los Angeles, he made sure to spread the credit to his collaborator. “I wrote a good screenplay,” he said, “but David Fincher made a great movie.”

headline.main: Disobeying Sorkin’s Musical Orders

docs.lead_paragraph: Fresh off a record-breaking Super Bowl Sunday audience of 111 million viewers, Fox delivered its best Monday night ratings of the season. According to Nielsen’s estimates, Fox’s “House” attracted its highest ratings of the season, with 12.3 million viewers at 8, while the network’s new crime drama “The Chicago Code” earned a solid start in its debut at 9, with 9.4 million. For the night over all, Fox ranked second to CBS and its comedy lineup. CBS’s “Two and a Half Men” drew the night’s largest audience, as usual, with 15.1 million viewers at 9, while “Mike & Molly” led at 9:30 with 12.7 million. CBS’s “How I Met Your Mother” (10.1 million) and “Rules of Engagement” (9.5 million) fared well at 8 and 8:30, while CBS’s “Hawaii Five-0” topped the ratings at 10 (10.9 million), outperforming ABC’s “Castle” (9.3 million) and NBC’s “Harry’s Law” (9.1 million). ABC finished a close third behind Fox, as an average of 9.7 million tuned in to “The Bachelor” from 8 to 10. NBC was fourth, with “Chuck” at 8 (5.4 million) and “Chase” at 9 (4.6 million).

headline.main: Fox Builds Night On a Strong ‘House’

docs.snippet: “Stephen Rodrick’s vivid picture of Marty Peretz underplays one ofthe man’s essential characteristics: his extraordinary kindness to young people.:
docs.lead_paragraph: Stephen Rodrick’s vivid picture of Marty Peretz underplays one ofthe man’s essential characteristics: his extraordinary kindness to young people. As a Harvard sophomore in the late ’60s, on scholarship in a place that could make you feel unnoticed, I took one of Peretz’s extraordinary seminars on McCarthyism. The recently departed ’50s seemed musty and irrelevant — until you sat down at one of Marty’s anything-goes lunchtime discussions, not only with people who had seen Communism as a genuine internal threat but also with others who had been blacklisted for years. Marty was available, enthusiastic, funny, biting, attentive to whatyou were doing and what you had to say. And yes, unorthodox in his opinions and relentless in probing yours. In other words, he was a thrilling teacher.

headline.main: Letters: Martin Peretz Is Not Sorry. About Anything.

docs.abstract: Sex-abuse scandals involving priests have shaken Ireland, but is that enough to break the grip of the Catholic Church?
docs.snippet: Sex-abuse scandals involving priests have shaken Ireland, but is that enough to break the grip of the Catholic Church?
docs.lead_paragraph: Andrew Madden is one of a relatively new breed of Irish celebrities who would just as soon be less well known. He was among the first people in Ireland to go public about being sexually abused by Catholic clergy — one of those who set off the intense bout of soul-searching that has racked the country lately. When I met Madden last fall in Dublin, the early rumbles of the collapse of Ireland’s economy were shaking the country, and throughout much of a pub lunch he talked about the failures of the government and the banks. It was only later, once we were driving around his old neighborhood, past the pebbledash house where he grew up and where his parents still live, that he began to talk about his childhood. As we sat in his car in front of Christ the King Church, where he spent much of his youth as an altar boy and a choir member, he outlined the four years of torment he suffered in the late 1970s at the hands of the Rev. Ivan Payne, one of the infamous serial sex offenders among the Irish Catholic clergy whose stories have transfixed the country over the past year and a half.

headline.main: The Irish Affliction

The store’s management said on Tuesday it would lay off 31 employees as part of its “response to the unprecedented, rapidly changing nature of the book industry.” Ryan Takas, the union representative for the employees who were laid off, said that the 31 employees make up more than 7 percent of the store’s 400-person unionized work force. Mr. Takas said that Powell’s had reduced its work force by about 40 employees in the last year through attrition, but still felt that layoffs were necessary because of a decline in sales of new books and a rise in health care costs. It was the first round of layoffs since the store’s workers formed a union in 2000.

headline.main: Powell’s Books Announces Layoffs

docs.lead_paragraph: There are moments, in the tumble of a typical improvisation, when the saxophonist Chris Potter seems to be embarked on a hero’s journey. With his strong, focused tone and top-to-bottom proficiency on the horn, he brings a robust physical presence to his playing and an onward-driving sense of purpose. His deployment of notes, parceled into staccato bursts or gracefully arcing phrases, suggests a split-second calculation of risk and reward. He works with an intuitive logic, venturing far from a theme and only gradually returning there, all the while responding to the changing conditions set by his band.

docs.snippet: Despite attracting 26.8 million viewers following the Super Bowl on Sunday, Fox’s hit musical series “Glee” drew only slightly better ratings than usual on Tuesday.
docs.lead_paragraph: Despite attracting 26.8 million viewers following the Super Bowl on Sunday, Fox’s hit musical series “Glee” drew only slightly better ratings than usual on Tuesday. According to Nielsen’s estimates 11.5 million tuned in to “Glee” at 8 p.m., up modestly from the 11.1 million who watched the show’s last Tuesday episode in December. Although “Glee” led the night among 18-to-49-year-old viewers, the show’s audience paled in comparison with the 20.3 million who watched CBS’s “NCIS” in the same time slot. CBS ranked No. 1 over all, winning both the 9 and 10 p.m. time slots with “NCIS: Los Angeles” (17.1 million) and “The Good Wife” (11.8 million). After “Glee” Fox earned lower ratings for its comedies “Raising Hope” (6.8 million) and “Traffic Light,” which garnered a disappointing 4.6 million viewers in its premiere at 9:30. NBC was third, and ABC placed fourth.

headline.main: ‘NCIS’ Lifts CBS

docs.lead_paragraph: A new application being sold on iTunes, “Confession: a Roman Catholic App,” cannot be used as a substitute for confession with a priest, the Vatican said Wednesday. The application was developed by American entrepreneurs with the help of two priests and the blessing of a bishop. It features a questionnaire of sins, and is promoted as a tool both to revive interest in confession and to help Catholics prepare for the sacrament. But some media reports cast the app as a “virtual priest” for Catholics who do not have time for church, prompting the Rev. Federico Lombardi, the Vatican spokesman, to respond, “One cannot speak in any way of ‘confession by iPhone.’ ”

headline.main: App Can’t Replace Confession, Vatican Says

docs.lead_paragraph: Sharp government spending cuts have forced contentious choices on local authorities, perhaps none more so than one council’s decision to heat a community swimming pool with energy diverted from a crematory. The council in Redditch, near Birmingham, has approved the diversion of waste heat from the crematory’s incinerator to a next-door leisure center and its new pool. Councilor Carole Gandy said the plan was consistent with the need for energy efficiency and had been widely backed by local residents once officials had explained the technology involved, which she described as common elsewhere in Europe. docs.snippet: If the street artist Banksy wins an Oscar, he will not be allowed up on stage in his usual costume of monkey mask, the Academy has said.
docs.lead_paragraph: The will-he, won’t-he riddle about Banksy and the Oscars – will he show up? won’t he be in disguise? – has a solution. After the Oscar nominees luncheon on Monday, Steve Pond reports, the Academy president, Tom Sherak, and executive director, Bruce Davis, “huddled at a table” with Jaimie D’Cruz, a producer of “Exit Through the Gift Shop,” Banksy’s Oscar-nominated documentary. They worked through the potential situations of Banksy winning and having to appear on stage, which he would presumably do in costume, his costume of choice being a monkey mask. Undignified, the Academy felt. “If Banksy isn’t comfortable showing his face on the Kodak stage, Sherak said, then the Academy isn’t comfortable having him on that stage,” Mr. Pond writes. Instead, the Academy officials and Mr. D’Cruz agreed, if the movie wins, Mr. D’Cruz will accept “without any additional shenanigans.”

headline.main: Banksy Shenanigans Not Welcome at Oscars

docs.abstract: Lynda Benglis, who has challenged the art establishment for decades, remains in the avant-garde. A retrospective of her work is being shown at the New Museum in New York through June 19.
docs.snippet: Lynda Benglis, who has challenged the art establishment for decades, remains in the avant-garde. A retrospective of her work is being shown at the New Museum in New York through June 19.
docs.lead_paragraph: LYNDA BENGLIS has gone her own way since first taking on the New York art world in the 1960s. She one-upped Jackson Pollock’s action paintings in the late 1960s by pouring pools of swirling pigmented latex directly on the floor and obscuring the distinction between painting and sculpture. She challenged the rigidity of Minimalism in the early ’70s with her hardened flows of polyurethane careening off walls and bristling with allusions to the body and landscape. She lampooned both the machismo of the art world and the way artists were expected to promote themselves in a market-driven system by exposing herself, with a dildo between her legs, in a 1974 Artforum advertisement that she paid for, earning her as many fans as detractors.

headline.main: A Life of Melting the Status Quo

docs.abstract: Wafaa Bilal, the New York University professor who had a camera inserted in the back of his head as part of an art project was forced to remove part of the camera on Friday because his body had rejected it.
docs.snippet: Wafaa Bilal, the New York University professor who had a camera inserted in the back of his head as part of an art project was forced to remove part of the camera on Friday because his body had rejected it.
docs.lead_paragraph: The New York University professor who had a camera inserted in the back of his head as part of an art project was forced to remove part of the camera on Friday because his body had rejected it, the Chronicle of Higher Education reported. The camera was to take a photograph every minute as the professor, Wafaa Bilal, went about his day. The project, which raised privacy concerns at the university, was called ”The 3rd I,” and was organized by a new Qatari museum called Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art. According to the Chronicle, the device, which was installed by a body modification artist in a tattoo shop in Los Angeles, was originally mounted on three posts that were attached to a titanium plate implanted between Mr. Bilal’s skin and his skull. But Mr. Bilal’s body rejected one of the posts, despite treatment with antibiotics and steroids, and he was in constant pain. So on Friday he had the post removed. While the wound heals, he is tying the camera to the back of his neck. Why didn’t he do that in the first place? “It’s a performance,” he told the Chronicle. “With the performance comes endurance. But also it’s a commitment. And I didn’t feel that strapping something around my neck would be the same.”

headline.main: No More Looking Backward: Professor Has Camera Removed From His Head

docs.abstract: The poems and songs of Tahrir Square directly challenge the official worldview propagated by the Mubarak regime.
docs.snippet: The poems and songs of Tahrir Square directly challenge the official worldview propagated by the Mubarak regime.
docs.lead_paragraph: The festive protests that broke out on Jan. 25 in Cairo’s Tahrir Square have become a window into what Egypt might look and sound like without the regime of Hosni Mubarak. Tahrir’s troubadour collective has specialized in the invention of slogans that are witty, abusive and aimed directly at the president, e.g., “Mubarak, you rhinoceros (kharteet), / get out, get out, you pest (ghateet).” Sometimes, perhaps to signal a certain gravitas, they dispense with rhyme and say it straight: “The people want the fall of the regime.” Along with the chanting, there has been much baladi music — a catchy, popular style, heavy on hooks and reverb — as well as poetry recitations and effigy hanging. This is Egypt’s folk culture: profane, bawdy, politically sophisticated. It stands as a direct challenge to the version of culture propagated by the Mubarak regime and its predecessors.

headline.main: Egypt: The Cultural Revolution

docs.lead_paragraph: The National Museum of African American History and Culture, the new Smithsonian museum set to open in 2015, has chosen a designer for its exhibitions. The museum has hired Ralph Appelbaum Associates, whose past projects include the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the William J. Clinton Presidential Center, several major permanent exhibitions at the American Museum of Natural History and the U.S. Capitol Visitor Center. In a conversation earlier this week, the museum’s director, Lonnie G. Bunch III, said that Mr. Appelbaum had brought together a group of young, culturally diverse designers to work on the project. The Smithsonian will pay Mr. Appelbaum’s firm roughly $3 million to design of the museum’s planned 82,000 square feet of exhibition space.

headline.main: Exhibit Designer Chosen for Museum of African American History and Culture

docs.lead_paragraph: Everything’s up to date in Cedar Rapids, which not only has skyscrapers, but also a hotel with a pool sparkling in the atrium like a blue diamond. For Tim Lippe (rhymes with yippee), the 34-year-old naïf at the center of this wistful, equally tender and raunchy comedy of self-discovery, also called “Cedar Rapids,” the hotel and the pool signal that he’s reached the big time. What he can’t yet know is that by entering the hotel, having guilelessly said no to the friendly neighborhood prostitute outside, he has crossed a Rubicon. He’s on his way to a moral awakening in a story laced with Oedipal overtones and giddy with longing and smut.

Sol and Miriam rarely spoke of past events, especially to their children, and their attitude created an air of secrecy that permeated the Salinger household and caused Doris and Sonny to grow into intensely private people.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Mr. Sunshine,” ABC’s new sitcom with Matthew Perry, made a promising start on Wednesday, even as Fox’s “American Idol” and its round of San Francisco auditions led the night with 23.7 million viewers, according to Nielsen’s estimates. The new ABC comedy drew 10.6 million viewers and delivered ABC’s best ratings of the season for a series premiere in the demographic of adults 18 to 49. The show benefited from a time slot following “Modern Family,” which earned 13.1 million viewers at 9 p.m., as well as from not having to compete directly opposite “Idol,” which trounced ABC’s sitcoms in the 8 p.m. hour, “The Middle” (8.8 million) and “Better With You” (6.8 million). ABC ranked third over all, struggling at 10 with “Off the Map” (5.6 million), while CBS trailed Fox in second place with strong results for “Criminal Minds” (14.3 million) and “Blue Bloods” (12.5 million).

docs.lead_paragraph: A human rights advocacy group based in the United States, China Aid Association, said Thursday that a human rights lawyer and his wife were severely beaten by security forces for having recorded a video revealing the details of the lawyer’s detention. The video of the blind Chinese rights lawyer, Chen Guangcheng, who has been under house arrest since he was released from prison last September, was posted by the rights organization on Wednesday. According to the video, 22 people have been assigned to watch Mr. Chen’s home in Shandong Province around the clock, he is not allowed to leave, cellphone calls cannot be made from the home and security officials bar any visitors. The organization said that Mr. Chen and his wife were beaten so severely they were not able to move from their bed, and they were denied the right to go to the hospital for medical care. Mr. Chen was sent to prison in 2006 for his human rights advocacy, and in particular for pointing out forced sterilizations and abortions in official abuses of China’s one-child policy.

docs.lead_paragraph: On Thursday night, at the start of Fashion Week, several hundred people came to the David Zwirner Gallery to see an exhibition of Philip-Lorca diCorcia’s photographs. Originally published in W magazine, between 1997 and 2008, the images are a remarkable record of a free-spirited period in publishing that seemed to come to an end with the recession and, as well, the Internet. They speak directly to the eye of Mr. diCorcia, with their capacity to excite and disturb, and to seek truth about human behavior in the most banal of scenes. These photographs were also the result of a fortuitous collaboration between Mr. diCorcia and Dennis Freedman, the former art director of W, who gave the artist carte blanche to shoot fashion stories in places like Havana, Cairo and New York. They have collected all 11 shoots in a new book, “Eleven” (Damiani Editions).

docs.lead_paragraph: Since January 2004, when this column first appeared, the American consumer zeitgeist has evolved. Some argue, in fact, that a decisive change has occurred, and that a result of the wrenching economic downturn is that we just don’t care about stuff anymore. I suspect this conclusion is rash. There are, however, interesting traces in the culture that suggest somewhat more subtle shifts — attempts, perhaps, to reconcile the more virtuously possession-resistant stance that some now strike with the stubborn reality that, ultimately, people really like stuff.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Aye, aye! they were mine — my irons, cried Ahab, exultantly. . . . Aye, I see — wanted to part it; free the fast fish — an old trick — I know him.” For a good generation now, the former chief of the C.I.A.’s bin Laden unit, Michael Scheuer, has insisted that he knew the tricks of Osama bin Laden, that he was on to him from the start, that he and the unit he headed from 1996 to 1999 had given the government multiple chances to kill or capture the Saudi master terrorist. The bureaucracy had not gone along; indecisive leaders who didn’t know the man they were trying to snag, who didn’t read his writings, had thwarted and betrayed the hunt. And still, after the calamities, after all the disasters inflicted upon us by this elusive and cunning adversary, we haven’t yet understood what we are up against. A view has crystallized that the trail of terror now goes beyond bin Laden, that the man on the run no longer pulls the strings of the jihad. Scheuer has come forth to challenge this complacency.

headline.main: Osama Bin Laden: The Specter

docs.lead_paragraph: Memoir has become in recent years a kind of hard-luck lit, and at first glance Henry Cockburn is just another young man dropped into trouble, as the sparks fly upward. Not that the particulars aren’t his own, or ­attention-grabbing. At 20, Cockburn hears a few trees request that he dance in some frostbiting February water. (“Oh that my words were now written!” even Job said. “Oh that they were printed in a book!” — so the confessional impulse, at least, isn’t entirely new.) Fishermen save Henry’s life; police officers reassign him from general to mental hospitals. He rides out the next seven years in more and more “secure” institutions, a prisoner guilty basically of skinny-dipping. The story is sad, but “Henry’s Demons” is more than just that.

docs.lead_paragraph: Nelson Mandela was circumcised as a 16-year-old boy alongside a flowing river in the Eastern Cape. The ceremony was similar to those of other Bantu peoples. An elder moved through the line making ring-like cuts, and foreskins fell away. The boys could not so much as blink; it was a rite of passage that took you beyond pain. They exclaimed, “Ndiyindoda!” (“I am the man!”). A brambly leaf was wrapped around the wound to stop the bleeding. The boys had to lie in a certain position, and at midnight they were woken. One by one, they went out into the cold and buried their foreskins in stony soil. For Mandela, the circumcision was something that linked him with his Thembu ancestors; in losing a part of his manhood, he became a man.

docs.lead_paragraph: From the very first sentence of his unusual memoir, “House of Prayer No. 2,” Mark Richard brings together the vernacular and the performative. “Say you have a ‘special child,’ ” the book begins, at once inviting us in folksy terms to suppose this to be the case and commanding us to summon the child into existence through the sheer act of saying so. The opening pages, Genesis-like, call the child’s world into being, his early life created via a series of severe directives: “Birth him with his father away” and “Move the family to a tobacco county in Southside Virginia” and “Make the ­mother cry and miss her mother.” The special child in question, we come to understand, is Richard himself. It’s an uncommon way to introduce the protagonist of a memoir, but an apt way to frame this absorbing account of growing up in the 1960s South, living with a disability, becoming a writer and finding faith. Richard’s book attests to the power of words (and the Word) in shaping a life, while at the same time challenging some dearly held beliefs about memoir as a genre.

docs.snippet: Four years ago, Ree Drummond was just another sometime city girl turned Oklahoma ranch wife with a flock of home-schooled children and a blog. Now, she’s a full-fledged media star.
docs.lead_paragraph: GREEN ACRES: Four years ago, Ree Drummond was just another sometime city girl turned Oklahoma ranch wife with a flock of home-schooled children and a blog. Now, she’s a full-fledged media star, with millions of page views a month at ThePioneerWoman.com, a long list of television appearances and a new memoir, subtitled “Black Heels to Tractor Wheels,” at No. 2 on the hardcover nonfiction list. (It’s also No. 8 on the e-book list, on Page 23.) Call Drummond the Prairie Dog Mother: she mixes the chipper can-do spirit of Laura Ingalls Wilder, the slick production values of Martha Stewart and steely domestic ambition that Amy Chua might approve. At her Web site, vicarious homesteaders can read instructions on topics ranging from how to load hay onto your feed truck and knock down fences to how to make Pasta ai Quattro Formaggi and spiff up digital photographs. (Photoshop’s “define and sharpen” feature is apparently “really good for animal hair.”) Drummond has said she started her blog mainly as a way of sharing photos with her mother. Now, she offers lavish down-home food porn like a 39-shot pictorial on “Perfect Potatoes au Gratin,” a perfect accompaniment to the copious beefcake shots of her Wrangler-rocking husband, a k a Marlboro Man, cuddling a baby or wearing chaps or “nourishing” cows, his face usually shadowed under the brim of a cowboy hat. “When my husband and I got married, we became one flesh,” Drummond wrote in a recent post. “So when he spends eight hours tearing down and building fence, it’s like I do, too. I just love the one flesh concept! It makes me one of the hardest workers I’ve ever met.”

docs.lead_paragraph: An exhibition of ancient Chinese artifacts will go forward at the University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archeology and Anthropology, after all. The exhibition, “Secrets of the Silk Road,” which includes materials, including two mummies, recently excavated at desert burial sites in western China, was organized by the Bowers Museum in Santa Ana, Calif., and was shown there last year and subsequently at the Houston Museum of Natural Science, where it closed on Jan. 2. It was scheduled to open at the Penn Museum on February 5, but last week, three days before the planned opening, the museum announced that China had requested that none of the artifacts be displayed. As a result, the museum would only show photographs, multimedia presentations, and a recreation of an excavation site; it offered refunds to those who had bought advance tickets and said that the exhibition would now be free.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Peter’s inspiration was a very fabulous American artist called Cindy Sherman,” said the (very fabulous French) makeup artist Tom Pecheux backstage at Peter Som. “She does self-portraits where she takes herself on a crazy journey. She always brings a twist into her face, so in terms of makeup we wanted to do that.” This translated into nearly nude skin (with a bit of rosy blush and a touch of shimmery powder topping cheeks), bare brows, lashes and eyelids, punctuated with a statement lip. “We started with a red lipstick, the definition of a grown-up woman,” said Pecheux, noting that the designer’s fall 2011 collection seemed more adult to him than previous seasons. “To twist it, we are adding a layer of metallic color.” Lips were lined with M.A.C. Cherry Lip Pencil, filled in with a lipstick color being tested for fall tentatively called Runaway Red (according to M.A.C., Dare You is the closest shade currently available), dusted with M.A.C. Invisible Powder, and then dabbed with M.A.C. pigments in silver, rose gold and melon. “I’m not a fan of a lip with shimmer, a frosted lip — I think it’s cheesy,” said Pecheux of his matte metallic creation. The look was paired with a hairstyle inspired by Tippi Hedren’s character in “The Birds,” using Wella Ocean Spritz for texture and extensions with roots dyed into them. “It gives the hairstyle depth, it makes hair look thicker, the minute you have a root it makes hair look thicker and a bit denser,” the hairstylist Eugene Souleiman, who crafted the look, explained of the extensions. “It’s a little like when I used to do Prada and Miu Miu. It has that ’90s take on the ’50s — it’s slightly minimal, but now it’s a bit more raw.”

docs.snippet: Two focus groups attended Thursday night’s performance, and four more are scheduled to be at Friday night’s show and the Saturday matinee.
docs.lead_paragraph: The going rate for your thoughts used to be a penny. Now the producers of the Broadway musical “Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark” are offering $60 goodie bags to people who serve in focus groups that will respond to several performances. Two focus groups attended Thursday night’s performance, and four more are scheduled to be at Friday night’s show and the Saturday matinee. It’s not unheard of for Broadway producers to use focus groups, and the musical has used them before since preview performances began on Nov. 28. But these are the first since largely negative reviews of the show by theater critics across the country were published on Tuesday. OnTrack Research, a marketing and consulting firm, is coordinating the focus groups, and here’s the rub: participants only get to see Act I or Act II, not both. They are then asked to fill out surveys and join in discussions in a “V.I.P. room.” The details of the focus groups were outlined in an e-mail to participants from OnTrack Research. Here is the full e-mail, which a focus group participant passed along and which was authenticated by the production on Friday.

headline.main: More Focus Groups for ‘Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark’

docs.abstract: Advanced stats show that Chris Bosh plays better from the right block than the left, but could Bosh’s awareness of that information have an unexpected negative impact on his performance?
docs.snippet: Advanced stats show that Chris Bosh plays better from the right block than the left, but could Bosh’s awareness of that information have an unexpected negative impact on his performance?
docs.lead_paragraph: The sports analytics movement has given basketball decision makers more valuable information than they have ever had, but, in a way, their experience in implementing their findings is atypical in the information age. The modern world is marked by the rapid dissemination of incredible amounts of information to relevant and interested parties; people from all over the planet know more today about one another and the world they inhabit than any human beings have before, primarily because of how freely information is exchanged. When it comes to analytical data in sports, however, coaches in particular face a unique challenge in passing along the statistical information they deem important. It’s not enough to know that a player is most effective running one type of play or shooting from one area of the floor. Coaches today must also understand how to convey that information in a way that makes it digestible and useful.

headline.main: Chris Bosh and the Self-Fulfilling Prophecy

docs.lead_paragraph: CRAMMED into this year’s field of 10 best picture Oscar nominees are British aristocrats, Volvo-driving Los Angeles lesbians, a flock of swans, a gaggle of Harvard computer geeks, clans of Massachusetts fighters and Missouri meth dealers, as well as 19th-century bounty hunters, dream detectives and animated toys. It’s a fairly diverse selection in terms of genre, topic, sensibility, style and ambition. But it’s also more racially homogenous  more white  than the 10 films that were up for best picture in 1940, when Hattie McDaniel became the first black American to win an Oscar for her role as Mammy in “Gone With the Wind.” In view of recent history the whiteness of the 2011 Academy Awards is a little blinding.
