docs.abstract: Yale University has signed a partnership agreement with a Peruvian university to establish a joint center for the conservation, study and display of Machu Picchu artifacts.
docs.snippet: Yale University has signed a partnership agreement with a Peruvian university to establish a joint center for the conservation, study and display of Machu Picchu artifacts.
docs.lead_paragraph: Three months after Yale University and the government of Peru announced a tentative accord under which Yale would return a group of artifacts excavated at Machu Picchu, Yale formally signed a partnership agreement on Friday with a Peruvian university to establish a joint center where the objects will be conserved, studied and displayed. The center will be at the Universidad Nacional de San Antonio Abad del Cusco, in Cusco, the city closest to Machu Picchu, and will be called the U.N.S.A.A.C.-Yale International Center for the Study of Machu Picchu and Inca Culture. It will include a museum exhibition space; a storage site for the archeological artifacts, which include stone tools, ceramics and human and animal bones; and a laboratory and research area. Students and faculty members from Yale are expected to visit the center for training, research projects and field work; students and faculty members of the Peruvian university will also visit Yale. Meanwhile, a small number of artifacts will be loaned to Yale for display at the Yale Peabody Museum of Natural History.

headline.main: Yale and Peru Sign Accord on Machu Picchu Artifacts

docs.abstract: The best of Nordic furniture, past and present, is on view at Stockholm Design Week.
docs.snippet: The best of Nordic furniture, past and present, is on view at Stockholm Design Week.
docs.lead_paragraph: In most people’s minds, there are only two settings on the Nordic furniture dial: Then (meaning postwar Modern) and Now. While I went to this year’s Stockholm Design Week, which ends on Sunday, excited solely about the latter, it turned out that the fair had something to offer in the former department as well. The Danish manufacturer Gubi recently shifted its attention towards resurrecting mid-century design icons, and the first fruits of that effort are on display this week. It has reissued Greta Grossman’s 1947 Grasshopper lamp and the 1966 Stokke Chair by Jens Qvistgaard, and is now the sole owner of reproduction rights for the cult Hungarian designer Mathieu Mategot’s work, starting with a multicolored coat rack and two pieces in his signature perforated metal: the Nagasaki chair and the Dedal bookcase. Mategot fans accustomed to 1stdibs sticker shock should rejoice.

headline.main: Stockholm Design Week | From Modern to Mod

docs.snippet: The editors on many of David Fincher’s movies talk about cutting down Aaron Sorkin’s “Social Network” script without cutting too far, the director’s superior visual sense and his habit of talking to himself.
docs.lead_paragraph: As a filmmaker, David Fincher has the reputation of an extreme perfectionist, so finely attuned to detail that he doesn’t trust anyone else to get even minor secondary shots. That vision earned him an Oscar nomination as the director of “The Social Network” – but what about the guys who have to work with him? While Mr. Fincher is celebrated for doing dozens and dozens of takes , what’s often forgotten is that other people then have to look at each and every one of those takes to put the film together. Apparently they don’t mind; the editors Kirk Baxter and Angus Wall, and the sound designer, editor and mixer Ren Klyce have all worked with Mr. Fincher multiple times, on films like “The Curious Case of Benjamin Button” and “Zodiac.” They are all Oscar-nominated for “The Social Network,” and are working with Mr. Fincher on his next film, “The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo.”

docs.abstract: A gem from the world of Japanese television and pop culture: Takarazuka is an all-women Vegas-style musical theater group, known for their adaptations of Western pop songs.
docs.snippet: A gem from the world of Japanese television and pop culture: Takarazuka is an all-women Vegas-style musical theater group, known for their adaptations of Western pop songs.
docs.lead_paragraph: For the modern YouTube hunter the world of Japanese television and pop culture can be a seemingly bottomless treasure trove. Among some of the finest gems are clips like the one above of Takarazuka, a 98-year-old Japanese song and dance troupe that specializes in performing adaptations of Western pop songs, classic musicals, operas, plays, novels or films as well as Japanese folk tales. (The clip above shows the musical number “The Great Century,” which incorporates the ’80s soft rock anthem “Final Countdown.”) But in a bizarre twist on the idea of an all-male Shakespearean cast, the members of the ensemble are all women — making Takarazuka perhaps the only Vegas-style musical theater group in the world with professional drag kings on permanent payroll. But despite appearances, Takarazuka was never meant as an early-20th-century chorus line for Japanese women’s liberation. To this day, cast members are put through a rigorous and patriarchally organized training program for several years before they are even allowed to set one foot on stage, with “female” (musumeyaku) and “male” (otokoyaku) actresses strictly separated in classrooms and dormitories. The inevitable lesbian overtones were largely ignored until the mid- to late 1930s, when Japanese officials were alarmed to a point that a ban on contact between the “male” cast members and their passionate female fans was imposed. To this day, most of Takarazuka’s over-2.5 million-strong annual audience consists of women, and so do the performers: an attempt in the 1940s to introduce male actors was successfully boycotted by Takarazuka’s own disgruntled cast.

headline.main: Kitsch of the Day | Takarazuka

docs.abstract: In a joint statement with Mr. Muti and officials of the orchestra, two cardiologists at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Donald Lloyd-Jones and Bradley P. Knight, reported on Friday that Mr. Muti had fainted because of “a common heart rhythm disturbance.”
docs.snippet: In a joint statement with Mr. Muti and officials of the orchestra, two cardiologists at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Donald Lloyd-Jones and Bradley P. Knight, reported on Friday that Mr. Muti had fainted because of “a c...
docs.lead_paragraph: The cause of Riccardo Muti’s fall from the podium during a rehearsal of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra on Feb. 3 has been determined. In a joint statement with Mr. Muti and officials of the orchestra, two cardiologists at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Donald Lloyd-Jones and Bradley P. Knight, reported on Friday that Mr. Muti had fainted because of “a common heart rhythm disturbance.” Although their tests reveal that he retains excellent heart function, they added, he has had a pacemaker installed to monitor his heart rhythm and deliver a small electrical charge if the heart rate should fall too low. “Patients with pacemakers live full and active lives with excellent prognosis,” the doctors concluded. Mr. Muti remains in Northwestern Memorial Hospital, where he is recovering from surgery for facial injuries incurred in the fall. He has canceled his remaining performances this winter, which were to run through Feb. 19. His next scheduled appearance with the orchestra is a concert performance of Verdi’s opera “Otello” on April 7, to be repeated twice in Chicago and, on April 15, in Carnegie Hall.

headline.main: Cause of Muti Collapse Determined

docs.abstract: Lakers Coach Phil Jackson, who says he is retiring, talks warmly of New York. Some wonder if he won’t resume his career there.
docs.snippet: Lakers Coach Phil Jackson, who says he is retiring, talks warmly of New York. Some wonder if he won’t resume his career there.
docs.lead_paragraph: There are few gaps in Phil Jackson’s cluttered coaching résumé. He has more N.B.A. championships than anyone and more victories than most. He won a title in the Continental Basketball Association, with the Albany Patroons. He even coached a few tours in Puerto Rico. Yet somehow, Jackson never made it back to his N.B.A. roots, back to his favorite city, back to the corner of 33rd Street and Eighth Avenue. Jackson interviewed with the Knicks three times over the last three decades but the timing was never right. In 1987, the Knicks passed up Jackson, then coaching the Patroons, to hire Rick Pitino. Jackson joined the Chicago Bulls’ staff. Twelve years and six championships later, Jackson — a free agent after leaving the Bulls — spoke with the Garden president Dave Checketts. The exploratory talks went nowhere and Jackson instead joined the Los Angeles Lakers. Jackson was a free agent again in 2005 when Isiah Thomas asked him to coach the Knicks. Jackson declined because he got a better offer: a return to the Lakers. Now 65, Jackson intends to retire from the N.B.A. after this season, and this time for good. The opportunity for a prodigal return has seemingly passed. But at least one authority on Jackson can still envision him joining the Knicks some day. “Phil is definitely a full-circle kind of a guy, and that would bring him full circle,” said Jeanie Buss, Jackson’s girlfriend and a Lakers executive.

headline.main: Phil Jackson’s Soft Spot for New York

docs.lead_paragraph: The radical art collective Voina has been shortlisted for a contemporary art award by Russia’s Ministry of Culture and the National Center for Contemporary Art for a project that consisted of a 210-foot penis painted on a drawbridge in St. Petersburg. The nomination came despite the fact that two of the group’s leaders await trial on hooliganism charges that could bring a sentence of up to seven years  the fallout from an action they called “Palace Revolution,” which involved running up to parked police cars and turning them upside-down. A St. Petersburg judge refused to grant bail for the two last month, despite an offer to pay from Banksy, the mysterious British street artist. Voina’s other actions have included an orgy in the State Museum of Biology and throwing live cats over a counter at McDonald’s, but they drew special attention for the drawbridge painting, which slowly rose to point at the St. Petersburg headquarters of the state security service, the F.S.B. docs.lead_paragraph: From the looks of their fall collection, this winter has taken a toll on Rag & Bone designers David Neville and Marcus Wainwright. “There’s a lot of shearling; it’s Eskimo-inspired,” said the makeup artist Gucci Westman backstage. “It’s makeup you would do if you were on a trek in Bhutan or something. Like you’d use eyeliner because you heard it would keep bugs away.” Unfortunately, at least for John Galliano during a damp summer, this last part is not true — but nonetheless, Westman’s handiwork, all done using the products she’s created with Revlon, is very pretty. “I’m using a purple lipstick on the bottom [lid] and then brown shadow over it, and then I’m using black liner to rim the eyes. I’m bringing the shadow down further than normal. The cheeks are just windswept; I’m using that same purple color all over the cheeks and the lips.” The hairstylist Guido Palau crafted very loose braids of varying thickness and number to go with the reference. “It’s very clean and natural,” he said. “I want it to feel hardly in there, so there’s a point of reference but it’s not overly anything–like when a girl starts braiding her hair by herself. It’s kind of an easy one.” Exactly what you’d want when hiking through the Himalayas or, you know, Brooklyn.

docs.lead_paragraph: For his fall men’s collection, the designer Richard Chai homed in on individuality, and the striking relationship between “unconventional beauties in refined clothes.” The hair stylist Kevin Ryan agreed backstage, explaining that “these men are not perfect, these are real men with flaws.” To create a “disheveled, slept-in feel,” Ryan first liberally applied Bumble & Bumble Surf Spray and Sumo Tech to create a matte, dry texture, then used his own R Session Tool “Root Control,” a ceramic heated comb, ideal for taming frizz and flyaway strands. And since the overall goal was to “make hair look rough and not too groomed,” styles were finished with spritzes of TIGI Rockaholic Dirty Secret Dry Conditioner. For mysterious, sultry eyes, the makeup artist James Kaliardos used M.A.C. Satin Taupe and Charcoal Brown eye shadows and M.A.C. Brush #213, which “created a smoky eye without looking like sharp eyeliner.” Kaliardos then pressed M.A.C.’s Brit Wit Creme Blush into models’ lips and cheeks, and patted M.A.C. Line Filler all over the face to minimize pores and even out complexion. Forgoing foundation altogether, Kaliardos used concealer minimally, to “veil the skin” and not disguise individual imperfections.

headline.main: Backstage Grooming | Richard Chai

docs.abstract: The rock-chick look was the inspiration behind the makeup at Altuzarra.
docs.snippet: The rock-chick look was the inspiration behind the makeup at Altuzarra.
docs.lead_paragraph: “It was kind of Kate Moss in her Johnny Depp days meets Oasis meets couture, to take the collection from a rock-n-roll feel to more of a womanly look,” explained the hairstylist Tina Outen of the directive that inspired the amorphous hair at Altuzarra. She was filling in on sound byte duty for Paul Hanlon, the show’s key hairstylist, who was busy presiding over the swarm of stylists — three per girl — busy scraping hair back from the face, dousing it in product (chief among them Frederic Fekkai Coiff Bouffant Lifting & Texturizing Spray Gel), clipping it into twists and coils, and setting with a blow-dryer. “When the clips come out, they’re going to start to destroy [the shapes] by pulling out pieces to make it more 3-D,” said Outen. “When [the models] are in the line, Paul’s going to do his magic.” In between, the makeup artist Tom Pecheux painted on a glamorous take on the ’90s Kate Moss cat-eye. “I was like, what is a young designer like? Who does he want to dress? And which kind of woman wants to wear a cool young designer? A rock chick,” said Pecheux. His take replaced that “rock chick” staple, black liquid liner, with M.A.C. Rich Purple Chromagraphic Pencil on the eye’s waterline and M.A.C. Keep It Cool Eye Shadow (available fall 2011), used to a soft liner effect, brushed out to the brows. “I went for silver on the inner corner of the eye, almost like a futuristic tear.” And the crimson lip? “It’s a huge controversy! docs.lead_paragraph: Derek Lam’s last few collections have been tailored and somewhat minimalist, the type of clothing that often gets paired with a nearly nude face and natural waves on the runway. But Lam hasn’t shied away from making beauty statements: most recently, the electric coral eyeliner and ’60s waves for spring 2011 created by the hairstylist Orlando Pita and the makeup artist Tom Pecheux, both of whom were on hand early on this Sunday morning to work that magic again. “The collection today is inspired by uniforms, so I did this school-girl uniform hairstyle, where the girl scrapes her hair back and puts a barrette in her hair,” explained Pita. “But we’re not doing the barrette, to keep it a bit more streamlined.” The hair was straightened with a T3 iron, pulled into a clean half-ponytail and set with T3 Control Hairspray. Pecheux created a slate gray smoky eye using silver and black Estee Lauder shadows (available this fall), which he paired with a nude matte lipstick, brow pencil, and Estée Lauder Bronze Goddess Soft Duo Bronzer. “Derek Lam’s clothes are very feminine and very luxurious, but very graphic and minimal at the same time,” said Pecheux, a sentiment that was echoed by the manicure Jin Soon Choi paired it with. “It’s a wintery white from Estée Lauder called Porcelain — very clean, minimalistic, bright white,” she said. “White nail polish works on short to medium length nails, and I did a round shape — I’ve done it at a lot of shows, it’s more feminine.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty | Derek Lam

docs.abstract: Even as scientific knowledge flourished in the 19th century, many naturalists remained steeped in racial prejudices and stereotypes.
docs.snippet: Even as scientific knowledge flourished in the 19th century, many naturalists remained steeped in racial prejudices and stereotypes.
docs.lead_paragraph: In 1859, Paul Du Chaillu, a young explorer of French origin and adopted American nationality, wandered out of the jungle after a four-year expedition in Gabon.  He brought with him complete specimens of 20 gorillas, an animal almost unknown outside West Africa.  The gorilla’s resemblance to humans astonished many people, especially after Darwin published “On the Origin of Species” later that year.  The politician Edwin M. Stanton was soon calling Abraham Lincoln “the original gorilla” and joking that Du Chaillu was a fool to have gone to Africa for what he could as easily have found in Springfield, Ill.But the more common way to deal with our resemblance to monkeys and apes then was to fob it off onto other ethnic groups — typically black people, or sometimes the Irish.  A few white scientists even purported to find physiological evidence, in the configuration of the skull, for classifying other races as separate species, not quite as far removed as Caucasians from our primate cousins.  This undercurrent of scientific racism would play out to devastating effect in Du Chaillu’s own life.

headline.main: Race, Sex and the Trials of a Young Explorer

docs.lead_paragraph: Because the theater and Hollywood composer Burton Lane wrote the music for only two major Broadway hits (“Finian’s Rainbow,” with lyrics by E. Y. Harburg, and “On a Clear Day You Can See Forever,” lyrics by Alan Jay Lerner), he is perennially treated as an also-ran in the pantheon of great American songwriters. docs.lead_paragraph: With its unhinged ballerinas, lurid hallucinations, surfeits of blood and makeup, and one mad mother, the film “Black Swan” is hard to match as catnip for satirists of camp. The downtown theater artist Jack Ferver and his QWAN (Quality Without a Name) Company will take a stab with “Swan!!!,” a parody of the 2010 movie that will be staged as a dramatic reading from March 10 to 12 at Performance Space 122 in the East Village. The show is a follow-up to Mr. Ferver’s “Notes!!!,” a like-minded treatment of the Judi Dench-Cate Blanchett film “Notes on a Scandal“ that developed a cult following during performances downtown last spring and fall. According to production notes “Swan!!!” focuses on the ballerina Nina (Natalie Portman’s role in the film, played here by Jenn Harris), who is “freaking out because she is crazy.” Also crazy is her mother, played by Randy Harrison of Showtime’s “Queer as Folk” (and Barbara Hershey in the movie); her “Swan Lake” choreographer; and a former prima ballerina. Mr. Ferver will play the “hot new bad ballet girl in town,” Lily (Mila Kunis in the film), who becomes Nina’s frenemy. Mr. Ferver said in an interview that he had not gone through legal hoops with the creators of “Black Swan” because he and his collaborators were “appropriating the work into a camp spectacle,” meaning that parody is protected under fair-use exceptions to copyright law. “It is going to be insane,” Mr. Ferver promised. “Black Swan” has been nominated for five Academy Awards, including best picture and best actress for Ms. Portman; the Oscars ceremony is Feb. 27.

From March 3 to 26 the Brick is hosting an Iranian Theater Festival with plays in Persian and English. The roster includes newly commissioned works from playwrights in Iran as well as plays by more established authors and groups, like the Iranian exile Assurbanipal Babilla‘s “Something Something Uber Alles” and “Two Stories That End in Suicide” by Piehole, an experimental theater group in Brooklyn. Audiences will also be able to see “The Hip-Hop Waltz of Eurydice” and “Quotations From a Ruined City,” two works by Reza Abdoh, an Iranian-born artist who died in 1995 at the age of 32. docs.abstract: As the “The King’s Speech” dominated the Bafta awards on Sunday night, a speech from its star was the highlight of the event.
docs.snippet: As the “The King’s Speech” dominated the Bafta awards on Sunday night, a speech from its star was the highlight of the event.
docs.lead_paragraph: It wasn’t a total rout for “The King’s Speech” Sunday night at the Baftas, the British version of the Oscars. The ur-British movie did take home trophies for best film, best British film, best original screenplay, best score and best acting prizes for Geoffrey Rush, Helena Bonham Carter and Colin Firth. But David Fincher won best director for “The Social Network,” which also took best adapted screenplay for Aaron Sorkin. Mr. Sorkin attended, Mr. Fincher did not – he’s shooting “The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo” – so his award was accepted by his stars Jesse Eisenberg and Andrew Garfield. But it was Mr. Firth’s speech that was the hit of the event in London on Sunday night. (Mr. Firth also won a Bafta last year, for “A Single Man.”)

headline.main: A Fateful Call for Colin Firth

docs.lead_paragraph: “I’m the sunny face of polygamy.” Let’s just acknowledge that this line, delivered by Margene, was surely the best of Sunday’s episode of “Big Love.” Margene, who is getting deeper into the crazy pyramid scheme that is Goji juice, has also become the spokeswoman for a family increasingly in crisis. But before we get to that and the impending divorce proceedings, I have a bone to pick with the haphazard unfolding of the episode. The matter of Alby hiring Verland to attack Don during his ice fishing trip felt random and pointless. This is the best way the writers could think of for Alby’s getting back at Bill for getting Lura away from him? Even as the scene was transpiring it seemed as if the writers were doing it on a lark and were fully conscious that the plotting was arbitrary and almost jokey. (The jaunty music accompanying the attack made this especially clear.)Also: Bill’s mother’s dementia isn’t feeling fully integrated either. Her dementia may be relevant to the season’s theme of the Henricksons’ general deterioration, but beyond that symbolic value, it’s hard to see how Lois’s condition will matter much to the final outcome of the show. Another plot development that felt half-baked was the sudden turnaround of Bill’s fate at the legislature. The tabling of the impeachment felt way too abrupt.

headline.main: ‘Big Love’ Watch: A Family in Crisis

docs.abstract: The designer Thakoon Panichgual wanted a bold, tribal look for the hair and makeup in his show.
docs.snippet: The designer Thakoon Panichgual wanted a bold, tribal look for the hair and makeup in his show.
docs.lead_paragraph: “I was really looking at tribes, at the different sorts of tribes and tribal sensibilities and habitual things tribes do, from the Masai tribe culture to the people during the Rococo period,” the designer Thakoon Panichgual said backstage before his fall show. “There was a sense of uniformity about the way that they were dressing.” This translated into a collection he described as “electric,” and for the hair and makeup, Panichgual said he decided to go for bold instead of tempering the clothes with a basic look. The makeup artist Diane Kendal used Nars Velvet Matte Lip Pencil in Dragon Girl on eyelids and on top of it, and applied three blushes — Desire, Taj Mahal and Exhibit A, in that order from inner lid to outer lid to an ombre effect — which she blended out past the bleached eyebrows. “We wanted to have that feeling of sun and hotness but then also exotic,” Kendal explained. The hairstyle created by Odile Gilbert using Kerastase products echoed that sentiment, with pieces provided by the designer weaved into a complicated-looking updo. Panichgual explained, “The hair is superslick — almost posh, really — in the front, and then it’s pulled back and it’s got this weird chignon whipped up with yarn and hats that we’ve cut up and put into the bun. There’s a reality base there, but it’s a bit hyper.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty | Thakoon

docs.abstract: A puzzle that highlights the interplay of order and randomness in choosing a song from a playlist for Valentine’s Day.
docs.snippet: A puzzle that highlights the interplay of order and randomness in choosing a song from a playlist for Valentine’s Day.
docs.lead_paragraph: Today is Valentine’s Day, a day when you want to set the romantic mood by choosing the perfect music. To inspire us, last night was one of the music world’s biggest nights: the Grammy Awards. All you have to do now is to pick the right songs – today’s digital musical players and smartphones make it a snap to select them from your playlist to suit every mood. But what if you were stuck with a player that (thanks to Apple’s marketing genius) makes a virtue of randomness, like the iPod shuffle? This is the conundrum that gives rise to a fascinating puzzle contributed by Dion Wong of Australia. Previously, in When Randomness Produces Certainty, we saw how randomness acting over and over can create order. The question that arises in Dion’s puzzle is: How can we optimally combine randomness and order? It’s a fitting question for today because, no matter how orderly a plan you might have made for a perfect Valentine’s Day, randomness might just intervene. And the connection of randomness to the Grammy Awards ceremony is clear too – what random pattern of clothes (or what passes for them) did Lady Gaga wear? That might take us too far afield, so without further ado, here’s the puzzle.

headline.main: Numberplay: The Musical Shuffle

docs.abstract: A dreadlocked, extremely tall fixture on the downtown Manhattan performance circuit talks about his musical background, his Curtis Mayfield cover and his song for Valentine’s Day.
docs.snippet: A dreadlocked, extremely tall fixture on the downtown Manhattan performance circuit talks about his musical background, his Curtis Mayfield cover and his song for Valentine’s Day.
docs.lead_paragraph: Artists as diverse as Ashford and Simpson, Lena Horne, Del Marquis of the Scissor Sisters and Bread and Puppet Theater have all had the pleasure of being sung to, backed by or collaborating with Xavier Smith, a dreadlocked, extremely tall (6’6″) fixture on the downtown Manhattan performance circuit. For the past several years, Smith — who grew up in New York, has a gently soulful voice and prefers to be called simply “Xavier” (“with a hard X,” he notes, “like Ex-ayvier”) — has produced a Valentine’s song as a love letter to his friends, fans and whomever he might have been in love with that year. It started in 2004 with a cover of the Beatles’ “In My Life,” and this year’s offering is a heartbreaking rendition of Curtis Mayfield’s “The Makings of You” set to a small orchestral arrangement. From Bushwick, Brooklyn, where Xavier lives with Dima, his once-vicious but now sweet Himalayan blue-eyed cat, Xavier told T why he does the yearly Valentine’s song.

headline.main: Asked & Answered | Xavier

docs.abstract: An inventory of the Egyptian Museum in Cairo has found that 18 valuable artifacts are now missing after a break-in on Jan. 28, Egypt’s antiquities minister, Zahi Hawass, wrote on his blog on Sunday.
docs.snippet: An inventory of the Egyptian Museum in Cairo has found that 18 valuable artifacts are now missing after a break-in on Jan. 28, Egypt’s antiquities minister, Zahi Hawass, wrote on his blog on Sunday.
docs.lead_paragraph: A full inventory of the Egyptian Museum in Cairo has found that 18 valuable artifacts are now missing after a break-in on Jan. 28, Egypt’s antiquities minister, Zahi Hawass, wrote on his blog on Sunday. Previously, Mr. Hawass had only said that objects were damaged. Among the most important of the missing items are a limestone statue of the god Akhenaten holding an offering table and a gilded wooden statue of Tutankhamen being carried by a goddess. On Monday, however, CNN reported that 2 of the 18 objects — a heart scarab and a funerary statuette of the nobleman Yuya — had been found on museum grounds. Mr. Hawass also said that a storeroom at Dahshur was broken into on Saturday night. He told Ahram Online that eight amulets were missing. Meanwhile, there were accounts on Twitter of protests outside the offices of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, the government body run by Mr. Hawass, who was appointed by former President Hosni Mubarak.

headline.main: Valuable Artifacts Missing From Egyptian Museum

docs.abstract: Few designers create pieces as timeless as Carolina Herrera, and backstage at her fall show, the beauty team was hard at work creating a look to match.
docs.snippet: Few designers create pieces as timeless as Carolina Herrera, and backstage at her fall show, the beauty team was hard at work creating a look to match.
docs.lead_paragraph: Few designers create pieces as timeless as Carolina Herrera, and backstage at her fall show, the beauty team was hard at work creating a look to match. The makeup artist Diane Kendal painted on what she called “a classic Carolina face”: black cream eyeliner on the top lash line only with a bit of a wing, M.A.C. Haute and Naughty Mascara only on outer lashes, M.A.C. Eye Gloss on lids and M.A.C. Blush in Angel on the cheeks. “On the lips we’re using a new [M.A.C.] color called Prince Noir, and we’re applying it with a lip brush and then blotting it with tissue so it gives a really beautiful stained burgundy look,” Kendal said. Nails were kept relatively short and painted with two coats of a shade from Creative Nail Design called Dark Ruby followed by a generous coat of Super Shiney Top Coat, “to contrast the matte textures such as fur, velvet, suede,” said CND’s Wanda Ruiz. The hairstylist Orlando Pita, who took the “big, beautiful necklines” into account when creating his polished, rolled bun-chignon hybrid using Moroccanoil products, clearly also had the Carolina Herrera client in mind. “I’ve seen messy updos for a long, long time, and I’m moving away from them,” he said. “This collection is too polished for that.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Unlike designers who approach collections with a particular theme or era in mind, Billy Reid, the recipient of this year’s CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund, designs his piece by piece, which explains his infectious passion for the unique. For his fall collection, Reid said backstage, “My focus was on construction, a lot of tailoring. I spent an inordinate amount of time perfecting each piece. My men’s looks are cleaner, with more subtle details than before.” In line with Reid’s penchant for individuality, the hairstylist Marcos Diaz created looks that were “groomed but not Don Draper.” Using just the newly launched Mat Forming Ground from Davines (a supermatte clay) and his fingers, Diaz formed a natural-looking side part and left the rest of the hair “dry-looking and clean.” Emphasizing approachability, Diaz said, “I’m interested in keeping hair more realistic, something you could easily create at home.” The makeup artist Nadine Luke relied on a few key players from M.A.C. and her belief of “a little goes a long way” for men’s makeup. Luke hydrated skin with Studio Moisture Fix, concealed as necessary, moisturized lips with Lip Conditioner, and tamed unruly brows with Brow Set (which she considers a guy’s “secret weapon,” as it instantly grooms both brows and mustaches). Luke finished the look with Mineralize Skinfinish, a shimmer-free bronzer that contours and provides a matte finish in a pinch, noting that “Billy Reid’s guy is someone you wouldn’t imagine grooming because he’s slightly rugged. But really, he’s a polished gentleman.”Runway slide show

docs.lead_paragraph: Given that practically every piece left to us by the French composer Hector Berlioz offers examples of his vivid, unruly imagination, it comes as no surprise that his Requiem, an 1837 adaptation of the Roman Catholic Mass setting, takes impracticality to an extreme virtually unknown in his day, and hardly more common in ours. docs.abstract: The video for the 21-year old French male model-singer’s first single is pop video cliché at its best.
docs.snippet: The video for the 21-year old French male model-singer’s first single is pop video cliché at its best.
docs.lead_paragraph: Lovers of all things Lagerfeld are already familiar with Baptiste Giabiconi, whether it’s from Chanel couture shows, where the 21-year-old French male model and muse to Kaiser Karl invariably closed the show by sashaying around the runway with a giant lion’s head, or frolicking in the hay with Lara Stone. Or they might know him from his various photo shoots (signés Lagerfeld, of course) or public outings with his septuagenarian mentor, including a memorable St. Tropez trip in the summer of 2010, when Giabiconi and Lagerfeld stopped by a local newsstand, dressed to the nines and trailed by hordes of paparazzi and curious tourists. But being the male face for Chanel, Fendi and Karl Lagerfeld (as well as starring in a Coca-Cola Light campaign) is apparently not enough for the slightly cross-eyed little Corsican that could; in late 2010 Giabiconi also embarked on a singing career and released his first single, “Showtime.” Even though the song has been out for a few months and enjoyed considerable chart success in France, it’s gone largely unnoticed by the American public. Granted, under normal circumstances the epic video (above) accompanying the release of the heavily auto-tuned single would not be considered kitsch; its Wild West theme, with Giabiconi saving a bodacious brunette from her abusive boyfriend, complete with explosive super powers in the Californian desert, is pop video cliché at its best. And Giabiconi’s English (“Woz wrong wiz you, man?”) is certainly better than Lady Gaga’s French. But the fact that it has Karl Lagerfeld’s blessing and the remote possibility of him doing a special cameo as a Bond-style villain makes it all the more enjoyable. That sadly doesn’t happen, but then again, Giabiconi knows how to keep us on our toes: the video ends with a promising “To be Continued.”

headline.main: Kitsch of the Day | Baptiste Giabiconi ‘Showtime’

docs.abstract: The makeup artist Francois Nars and the hairstylist Guido Palau discuss their inspirations, backstage at the Marc Jacobs show.
docs.snippet: The makeup artist Francois Nars and the hairstylist Guido Palau discuss their inspirations, backstage at the Marc Jacobs show.
docs.lead_paragraph: “You know those old women in the street who are a little bit eccentric? There’s always one living next to you. They put too much blush on and they don’t do their eyeliner quite well, but it looks fabulous in the end. That’s what the idea was,” explained the makeup artist François Nars backstage at the Marc Jacobs show. This translated to a black eyeliner NARS is releasing this fall called Via Venetto applied with a downward curve (“the opposite of Audrey Hepburn’s look,” explained Nars) and NARS Lokum Cream Blush applied low, near the mouth. “I think it looks like a grandmother who put lipstick on her cheeks,” said Nars with a laugh. The hairstylist Guido Palau gave this aging glamor girl a Croydon facelift, creating what he called “a dominatrix ponytail” using Redken Blow Away, a gel for blow-drying, and Shine Flash for serious gloss (models wore berets made of PVC by the milliner Stephen Jones secured with black chin straps). Nails were painted a shiny peach Jacobs chose from the polish brand Zoya. “Marc is very hands on,” said the manicurist Elisa Ferri, pun unintended. “He has an amazing eye.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty | Marc Jacobs

docs.lead_paragraph: Senator John Kerry traveled to Pakistan late on Monday to help defuse a diplomatic furor over the arrest of an American official accused of murder, White House and Senate officials said. Senator Kerry, Democrat of Massachusetts, the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, planned to meet with senior Pakistani officials, and his visit was being coordinated with the White House. Tensions have been rising between the United States and Pakistan over the case of Raymond A. Davis, an American official who killed two motorcyclists in Lahore on Jan. 27 while driving his car. American Embassy officials say that Mr. Davis fired in self-defense when two armed men tried to rob him, but prosecutors in Pakistan have charged him with murder. American officials have insisted that he is protected by diplomatic immunity and should be released.

docs.abstract: The foundation of the Broadway director Arthur Laurents and his longtime partner, Tom Hatcher, announced on Tuesday that its first playwriting award, worth $150,000, would go to Jeff Talbott.
docs.snippet: The foundation of the Broadway director Arthur Laurents and his longtime partner, Tom Hatcher, announced on Tuesday that its first playwriting award, worth $150,000, would go to Jeff Talbott.
docs.lead_paragraph: The foundation of the Broadway director Arthur Laurents and his longtime partner, Tom Hatcher, announced on Tuesday that its first playwriting award, worth $150,000, would go to Jeff Talbott, a New York City actor who has branched out and will make his Off Broadway debut as a playwright next season. The award, which is to be given annually, provides $50,000 to the writer and $100,000 toward the production costs for mounting the recipient’s play. Mr. Talbott’s winning play, “The Submission,” described as an exploration of the importance of cultural authenticity in authorship, will be produced next season at MCC Theater, which is led by Robert LuPone, Bernard Telsey, and William Cantler. The Laurents/Hatcher Foundation Award is among the most generous in playwriting, and it is intended for emerging writers. Mr. Talbott, 46, has written only a few plays and, as a playwright, still lacks an agent. Mr. Laurents, the book writer for “Gypsy” and “West Side Story” and the Tony Award-winning director of the original “La Cage aux Folles,” created the award last year. At 93, he is still writing plays himself; Mr. Hatcher, his partner of 52 years, died in 2006.

headline.main: Laurents-Hatcher Award Announced

docs.abstract: An election year looms, as does the return of “Gore Vidal’s The Best Man,” the deliciously tart (when done well) play about politics, campaigns and the presidency.
docs.snippet: An election year looms, as does the return of “Gore Vidal’s The Best Man,” the deliciously tart (when done well) play about politics, campaigns and the presidency.
docs.lead_paragraph: Are the Iowa presidential caucuses really less than a year away? How time flies. But an election year looms, as does the return of “Gore Vidal’s The Best Man,” the deliciously tart (when done well) play about politics, campaigns and the presidency. Jeffrey Richards and his fellow producers announced on Tuesday that they would revive that 1960 play in the spring of 2012 with hopes of catching election fever. Originally titled “The Best Man,” Mr. Vidal’s play involves a showdown at a presidential convention between two candidates, in essence an Adlai Stevenson character and a Richard Nixon type, brokered by an ill ex-president and complicated by secrets, machinations, and troubled marriages. Broadway had a revival of “The Best Man” not so long ago, during the campaign between George W. Bush and Al Gore and the subsequent legal battle in the fall of 2000. With political resonance and a cast led by Spalding Gray, Chris Noth, and Charles Durning, that production started off strong at the box office but had mixed reviews and declining ticket sales before closing in late December. (Mr. Gore had conceded two and a half weeks earlier.) That 2000 revival was the first Broadway producing credit for Mr. Richards, who has been a press agent since the 1970s and is now one of Broadway’s busiest producers. He is reuniting his producing team from 2000 — Jerry Frankel, Michael B. Rothfeld, and Darren Bagert — to mount this production. The director will be Michael Wilson (“The Orphans’ Home Cycle,” “Dividing the Estate”). No cast members have been announced.

headline.main: Gore Vidal Political Play Returns

docs.lead_paragraph: As reports of the riots in the Middle East continue to flood news outlets, I follow with a distance that is rather peculiar considering my history and interests. Having spent nearly seven months of my four years at West Point in Egypt and Tunisia, I hold a special place in my heart for the people of both countries. After all, they helped me learn their language, and thus gave me a conduit to understanding the depths of one of the world’s most misunderstood regions. And while a call for liberation is certainly worthy of praise, it’s difficult for me to feel proportionally excited for my friends in Egypt and Tunisia, because there is a third country close to my heart that few have considered in this equation: Afghanistan.

docs.lead_paragraph: Tariq Tapa’s debut feature, “Zero Bridge,” begins promisingly with a Kashmiri teenager being schooled in petty crime, a scene that’s reminiscent of the Chinese director Jia Zhang-ke’s “Unknown Pleasures” in its immediacy and bleak authenticity. The film loses momentum after that, handicapped by Mr. Tapa’s sometimes sketchy screenplay and the limitations of his nonprofessional cast. (His clumsy staging of their dialogue scenes doesn’t help.) But it remains a moving slice of life from a corner of the world usually seen only in news reports or as a mountainous backdrop for Bollywood musicals.

docs.snippet: A blackout during protests has mesmerized technical experts and raised concerns about other governments.
docs.lead_paragraph: Epitaphs for the Mubarak government all note that the mobilizing power of the Internet was one of the Egyptian opposition’s most potent weapons. But quickly lost in the swirl of revolution was the government’s ferocious counterattack, a dark achievement that many had thought impossible in the age of global connectedness. In a span of minutes just after midnight on Jan. 28, a technologically advanced, densely wired country with more than 20 million people online was essentially severed from the global Internet.

docs.lead_paragraph: Israel temporarily closed four of its diplomatic missions abroad in recent days because of suspicions that they were under threat of attack, an Israeli official said on Tuesday. He refused to specify their locations, for security reasons, but he said that two had partially reopened. The precautions were taken after “unusual occurrences were identified recently around a few missions abroad,” the Israeli government said in a statement. The Israeli Counter-Terrorism Bureau had issued a travel advisory on Friday warning of a heightened threat against Israeli and Jewish targets abroad because of anniversaries this week of the deaths of two senior Hezbollah figures. It listed Egypt, Turkey, Georgia, Armenia, Ivory Coast, Mali, Mauritania and Venezuela as countries with a heightened risk. Imad Mugniyah, a Hezbollah commander, was killed by a bomb in Damascus in February 2008, and Hezbollah blamed Israel for his death. Sheik Abbas Musawi, a leader of Hezbollah, was killed by Israeli forces in February 1992.

headline.main: Israel: Four Foreign Missions Closed

docs.lead_paragraph: Last week, the multitalented Amber Martin wrapped up a four-week run of her latest show, “Amber Alert,” in front of a sold-out house at the Wild Project in the East Village. Martin seamlessly floated between multiple costumes, personae and skits, never once leaving the stage, and carrying the calm of a seasoned performer through comedic routines, duets and classic vocal covers. Martin’s first such transformation was from “Daydra,” a walking trailer-trash disaster complete with raspy smoker’s voice and greasy mullet, into the very vision of a solo diva, in a floor-length gown and heels, launching into a pitch-perfect rendition of Dionne Warwick’s first hit, “Don’t Make Me Over.” Guest performers included the Scissor Sisters frontman Jake Shears, the hysterical Bridget Everett and the gender-bending guitarist NathAnn Carerra, with whom Martin performed a very curious duet.

docs.lead_paragraph: For any savvy operagoer, an evening spent with “The Bartered Bride,” a rustic comedy by Smetana more widely known about than actually seen, is an evening spent waiting for the other shoe to drop. Introduced in 1866 and completed in 1870, this romantic frolic is built on a plot twist predictable from miles away, a triumph of true love over cynical calculation. The ending is never in doubt, yet the opera remains irresistible for its charming characters and lively pace, and, above all, for its rich, colorful score: part bubbly operetta, part Bohemian folk pageant.

docs.abstract: Makeup artist Dick Page and hairstylist Eugene Soulemain discuss their inspiration for the Narciso Rodriguez runway show.
docs.snippet: Makeup artist Dick Page and hairstylist Eugene Soulemain discuss their inspiration for the Narciso Rodriguez runway show.
docs.lead_paragraph: “We’ve never done anything like this at Narciso,” the hairstylist Eugene Soulemain said backstage at the Narciso Rodriguez show. “I scared the life out of him.” The style, a simple and somewhat haphazard knot just above the nape of the neck, was roughed up further with the addition of a few pats of Wella Professionals Texture Touch pressed in near the hairline, followed by a few spritzes of Wella Professionals Shimmer Delight “to make it look like she’s been running and sweating.” Soulemain said the edgier cast of models, which included Jamie Bochert (who had never walked for Rodriguez), inspired the look. “Even though the clothes are incredibly expensive, not everything’s pretty and so fitted,” Soulemain explained. “It’s not a red-carpet feeling.” Clearly, Rodriguez was convinced, seeing as he rang the manicurist Deborah Lippmann at 3 p.m. yesterday with some color direction. “He said, ‘I want a color that’s not charcoal and not blue and not black, but strong’ — they wanted to have some strength and toughness,” Lippmann said. (The gray she created will be named by Rodriguez and produced later this year.) The makeup artist Dick Page lined eyes with Shiseido cream shadows in Purple Dawn and Caviar, a black (available this fall). “I’m trying to leave the skin alone as much as possible. Since we’re at the beginning of the season, there are no big skin disasters yet,” Page said, joking that his own disaster — a black eye he acquired last week — inspired the look. One skin care product even made it onto models’ faces: Shiseido Benefiance Full Correction Lip Treatment, which was smudged onto the lids just before the show to create a melty effect. “It’s a ridiculously expensive lip balm,” Page said (it’s $36). What, you expected the Narciso woman to use Carmex?

headline.main: Backstage Beauty | Narciso Rodriguez

docs.abstract: At New York fashion week, everyone from Alexander Wang to Victoria Beckham is sporting the same thing — a fruity yet rich Bordeaux.
docs.snippet: At New York fashion week, everyone from Alexander Wang to Victoria Beckham is sporting the same thing — a fruity yet rich Bordeaux.
docs.lead_paragraph: As the New York shows approach the finishing line, it would seem that everyone from Alexander Wang to Victoria Beckham is serving the same thing for winter — a fruity yet rich Bordeaux. The color has been brightened and lightened, making it appear more like a Beaujolais nouveau rather than a deeper Pauillac, with bursts of fuchsia in the mix to provide balance. Although it appeared on upper-length leather gloves and platforms on heels, designers sought to liven up their looks with a new color. Olivier Theyskens’s second collection for Theory took a traditional approach with his wine-colored chunky knits, while Marc Jacobs played with the shade in all textures and lengths ranging from a pailette knee-length skirt to a pleated maxi version. The newcomer Prabal Gurung showed all varietals in a color-saturated fur coat over a sheer black dress, but no one did it like Posh, who provided standouts in the form of loose dresses in cashmeres and double-faced wools. As they say in Paris, santé!

docs.abstract: Smokey Robinson, who first performed at the Apollo in the 1960s as part of a Motown review, returned with a voice that still provides carnal assurance.
docs.snippet: Smokey Robinson, who first performed at the Apollo in the 1960s as part of a Motown review, returned with a voice that still provides carnal assurance.
docs.lead_paragraph: Smokey Robinson said he was “tripping” to be back performing at the Apollo Theater on Tuesday night, calling the theater “the real beginning of my show business life.” He reminisced about doing five shows a day there as part of Motown’s “Motortown Revue” in the early 1960s, when the Apollo crowds’ reputation for booing acts offstage was so fearsome, Mr. Robinson said, that “I was afraid to look out in the audience.” Now, a few days before his 71st birthday on Saturday, Mr. Robinson wasn’t just engaging the audience. He was trusting it, and seducing a good part of it. What might have been an oldies show became a singer’s teasing, obsessive tour de force.

headline.main: Motown at the Apollo, Suspended in Time

docs.abstract: New York City Ballet has performed Balanchine’s “Divertimento No. 15” this month, a ballet that has the most sublime choreography ever made to music by Mozart.
docs.snippet: New York City Ballet has performed Balanchine’s “Divertimento No. 15” this month, a ballet that has the most sublime choreography ever made to music by Mozart.
docs.lead_paragraph: High among my memories of the most illustrious dance performances are those that New York City Ballet gave in the early 1980s of Balanchine’s “Divertimento No. 15.” This ballet, with the most sublime choreography ever made to music by Mozart, creates an ideal realm in which courtesy, chivalry, brilliance, serenity and expansiveness coexist and give off light. In those performances, Balanchine style was at a peak of refinement: resplendent in line, dazzling in speed, calm in phrasing, tingling in musical precision. The huge box of stage space around the dancers was animated by their ardent three-dimensional physicality and their dynamics.

headline.main: Kaleidoscopes of Patterns Against Backdrop of Mozart’s Chivalry

One of her great later songs, for which she accompanied herself on piano, “The Blizzard” describes a brokenhearted woman driving alone through a winter storm in the Colorado Rockies and taking shelter with a stranger with whom she has a healing romantic encounter. The next morning she awakens in dazzling sunlight and continues her journey through the mountains, her faith in herself restored.

docs.abstract: Rahm Emanuel’s hard-won campaign to reclaim his Chicagoness.
docs.snippet: Rahm Emanuel’s hard-won campaign to reclaim his Chicagoness.
docs.lead_paragraph: On a brutally cold morning in mid-December, Rahm Emanuel, hatless and wearing a glove on only his left hand, stood for an hour in front of the turnstiles at the Paulina el station, which sits in his old Congressional district on Chicago’s North Side. As the trains slammed and screeched overhead, he offered his hand to the mostly young and professional commuters heading downtown. Emanuel’s manner seemed more studied than spontaneous. He employed standard lines — “nice hat,” “good book” — and relied on the logos on riders’ head wear and jackets for conversation starters. He addressed both sexes as “man,” and when a woman asked about his plans for the Chicago Transit Authority, he was characteristically a trifle abrupt — “Here’s the deal,” he said to start — and egocentric. As he did with me, he told her the elevated line right above us was something “I built,” before saying “we,” apparently realizing he was discounting the work and leadership of many others. He hardly seemed like an irresistible force.

headline.main: The One-Man Political Machine

docs.abstract: A statue of the pharaoh Akhenaten, one of the most valuable objects revealed earlier this week to have been stolen from the Egyptian Museum, has been found.
docs.snippet: A statue of the pharaoh Akhenaten, one of the most valuable objects revealed earlier this week to have been stolen from the Egyptian Museum, has been found.
docs.lead_paragraph: Zahi Hawass, the Egyptian antiquities minister, said on Wednesday that a statue of the pharaoh Akhenaten holding an offering table, left, one of the most valuable objects revealed earlier this week to have been stolen from the Egyptian Museum, had been found. In an interview, Mr. Hawass also defended himself against charges that he did not report the missing objects promptly. In the days after the museum was broken into on Jan. 28, Mr. Hawass claimed that, while 70 artifacts had been damaged, none had been stolen. Last Sunday he said that, in fact, 18 objects were missing from the museum. Two of the other objects, a heart scarab and a funerary statuette, as well as the goddess from a statue of a goddess carrying Tutankhamen, were found earlier this week. The Akhenaten statue was found in the garbage near Tahrir Square, Mr. Hawass said, by a boy whose uncle was a professor at the University of Cairo. “His uncle called me today, and I sent some of the police and archaeologists, and they found it is the statue of Akhenaten,” Mr. Hawass said. “We are going to look inside all the garbage that they collected from Tahrir Square to find the rest of the objects.”

headline.main: Stolen Egyptian Statue Is Found in Garbage

A fashion lover who’s usually clad in cutting-edge ensembles by Azzedine Alaïa, Haider Ackermann and Rick Owens, she often gets stopped in shops and restaurants by women who want to know where she got her jewelry. “I’ve been tempted to sell things right off my body,” she jokes. Instead, she mixes diamonds, sapphires and amethysts with moodier materials like jasper “zebra” agate, purple turquoise, Nubian opals and moonstones. “My pieces are a bit dark, but dark in a sophisticated way.” The earrings above are $16,105 at Ikram, in Chicago.

docs.snippet: In the last few days, several pieces by the British street artist Banksy have appeared around the Los Angeles area: a urinating dog, a mischievous Charlie Brown and a drunk Mickey and Minnie Mouse, with the slogan “Living the Dream.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Banksy has made it to Hollywood, or at least some of his work has. In the last few days, several pieces by the British street artist have appeared around Los Angeles: a urinating dog (placed in Beverly Hills), a mischievous Charlie Brown and a drunk Mickey and Minnie Mouse, with the slogan “Living the Dream.” (All the images are viewable on Banksy’s Web site.) Though Banksy’s reps confirmed to The Los Angeles Times that the work belonged to him, they did not mention whether it was part of his ongoing un-campaign for his Oscar-nominated documentary, “Exit Through the Gift Shop.” But since Banksy rarely does anything without it being carefully thought out, we can assume it’s more than a coincidence.

headline.main: Banksy Sightings in Hollywood (of a Sort)

docs.lead_paragraph: IT’S true that 59 sounds ancient for a dancer, but the sight of Vicky Shick might change your mind. The lithe Ms. Shick has been dancing for most of her life, something that over the years has appeared only more effortless. She possesses the kind of considered grace that comes from another world  she was born in Hungary  and perhaps another time.

docs.abstract: Alina Cojocaru, who will appear as a guest artist with American Ballet Theater, and Lauren Lovette, who has a principal role with New York City Ballet, are dancers to watch for this season.
docs.snippet: Alina Cojocaru, who will appear as a guest artist with American Ballet Theater, and Lauren Lovette, who has a principal role with New York City Ballet, are dancers to watch for this season.
docs.lead_paragraph: ALINA COJOCARU is a ballerina who makes you understand why that title should be reserved for a select few. Of course she has a fabulous classical technique and a beautiful line. Of course she has a weightless, airy jump and limpid, exquisite arms. Of course she is both musical and a superb actress. But Ms. Cojocaru, a Royal Ballet principal who will appear as a guest with American Ballet Theater this season, is even greater than the sum of those parts. In her heart-wrenching portrayal of a simple peasant girl betrayed by the man she loves in “Giselle”; in the extreme, imploding articulations of Wayne McGregor’s “Chroma”; or as the radiantly youthful princess of “The Sleeping Beauty,” she brings an ineffable combination of steely strength and lyrical delicacy to her dancing that is ever-changing and ever-fascinating.

docs.lead_paragraph: AMID the world’s wide range of illustrious dancers, I draw attention to a rare species that may soon become extinct: the Merce Cunningham performer. Since Cunningham’s troupe’s began in 1953 it has consistently contained a number of the world’s most extraordinary dancers. But on New Year’s Eve, at the end of the two-year Legacy Tour, the Merce Cunningham Dance Company gives its final performance, and nobody knows yet if much of his choreography will survive in performance anywhere.

headline.main: A Grand Finale: Cunningham’s Last Dances

docs.abstract: The hairstylist Paul Hanlon discusses the inspiration behind the runway looks for the Fall 2011 show.
docs.snippet: The hairstylist Paul Hanlon discusses the inspiration behind the runway looks for the Fall 2011 show.
docs.lead_paragraph: Fashion’s latest hairstylist darling, the charming Paul Hanlon, knows the Proenza Schouler girl quite well. Last season, he imagined she’d fallen asleep on a bus, and created what was meant to look like a French twist that had been battered by a long day (and a long commute, one assumes). This season, she’s grown her hair nearly to her elbows (Hanlon used 22-inch extensions) and pulled it into a low ponytail with some knotty nubs at the end. “When [designers Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez] called me in London, the first thing they said to me was that they loved the idea of the girls having really long hair. The first test we did, the girls had this really long straight hair, very blunt, but it didn’t feel like their woman — it was a bit army,” said Hanlon, adding that the boys were inspired by a cross-country road trip they’d just been on. As an alternative, Hanlon referenced photographer Edward S. Curtis’ portraits of American Indian women, their hair parted in the middle, heavy behind their shoulders. He began a very low braid, which he then tied with a black elastic, leaving the last loop halfway pulled through. After the tips of the hair were razor cut, the entire head was sprayed with Frederic Fekkai Sheer Hold Hairspray (through a net, a favorite Hanlon technique) for some “crunch.” “It’s like when girls go out and they leave their ponytail tucked into their jackets, and when they take it off it looks kind of wrong. I’m looking around at Diane’s assistants,” Hanlon said, referring to the makeup artist Diane Kendal, “and some of them walked in with their hair like that. It’s nice to have a wearable look. Hairstylists get a bit carried away sometimes.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty | Proenza Schouler

docs.snippet: This weekend marks the kickoff of Modernism Week, Palm Springs’s annual celebration of all things midcentury modern.
docs.lead_paragraph: This weekend marks the kickoff of Modernism Week, Palm Springs’s annual celebration of all things midcentury modern. One of its highlights is “Steel and Shade: The Architecture of Donald Wexler,” an exhibition at the Palm Springs Art Museum. Wexler, 85, has practiced in Palm Springs for almost six decades, developing an architecture that is acutely sensitive to the extremes of the desert climate. Wexler’s all-steel Alexander houses, designed in 1962 with the structural engineer Bernard Perlin for the developers George and Robert Alexander, were sustainable before sustainability was trendy. Affordable, elegant and quick to assemble on site, thanks to a prefabricated structural system, Wexler’s houses (their framing, roofs and exterior siding are steel, with drywall interior siding) were the perfect answer to the postwar housing boom. “Steel, concrete and glass are ideal materials for the desert,” Wexler says. “They are inorganic and don’t deteriorate in the extreme temperatures of the desert.” And since these structures are relatively maintenance-free, the seven Alexander houses in a north Palm Springs enclave are as pristine today as they were almost 50 years ago.

headline.main: Seeing Things | Donald Wexler, Desert Modernist

docs.lead_paragraph: There is a situation in chess called zugzwang in which any legal move leaves the player worse off (in other words, he’d be better off to pass his turn). Oftentimes, in fact, the zugzwang is mutual: both players would rather that the other one move next. A typical situation — black’s only legal move would lead to a loss, but white’s only legal moves would turn an advantageous position into a draw — is illustrated below.

docs.abstract: Anchored by the immense L.A. Live entertainment complex, the long-blighted downtown has become an accessible, pedestrian-friendly destination.
docs.snippet: Anchored by the immense L.A. Live entertainment complex, the long-blighted downtown has become an accessible, pedestrian-friendly destination.
docs.lead_paragraph: THE sprawl, the scale, all that freeway time — for many, Los Angeles is an acquired taste. But not downtown. New York-like in its density and mishmash, the long-blighted center has become an accessible, pedestrian-friendly destination in recent years; Angelenos walk around en masse, using their actual legs. The immense L.A. Live entertainment complex is largely responsible for this comeback, but the studiously vintage bars and imaginative restaurants that seem to open every other day are also part of the revival. Skid Row and the drifts of homeless camps haven’t vanished altogether, and the grittiness still varies by block. But this part of town is alive again, in ways that make sense even to an outsider.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Downtown Los Angeles

docs.snippet: The photographer Danielle Levitt discusses her new show, “Pride of Lowell,”  at Los Angeles’s Known Gallery.
docs.lead_paragraph: The photographer Danielle Levitt has an eye for disaffected youth. Her 2008 monograph “We Are Experienced” compiled more than 100 portraits of American teenagers taken over several years as Levitt hopscotched across the country shooting features and fashion editorials for Interview, Arena Homme Plus and The New York Times Magazine, among many others. Levitt began her career shooting a street style column for The Wall Street Journal, a natural window onto the downtown scene, and her work has evolved to include “werewolves” in Texas for Dazed & Confused and sissy bouncers for Arena Homme Plus. This fall, she was sent to Lowell, Mass., to shoot Mickey Ward and Dicky Eklund, the real-life characters behind David O. Russell’s Oscar-nominated film “The Fighter”; the magazine assignment turned into a new series of portraits and a collection of short films. “Pride of Lowell,” curated by Naheed Simjee, will opened on Wednesday at Los Angeles’s Known Gallery. T caught up with Levitt via e-mail to talk about the show.

headline.main: Fight Club | Danielle Levitt’s ‘Pride of Lowell’

docs.snippet: The makeup artist Aaron de Mey discusses the inspiration behind the looks for the L’Wren Scott runway show.
docs.lead_paragraph: “A dangerous eye — that’s what L’Wren said to me,” said the makeup artist Aaron de Mey backstage at L’Wren Scott. “It conjured up images of smokiness. I also love this kid Taylor Momsen very much — it’s interesting to see how a teenager would apply her makeup.” To wit, de Mey created an exaggerated version of the kind of black eye makeup he said Scott herself always wears, which included heaps of Lancome Hypnose Mascara (in black, of course) and black eye shadow layered over pencil for a gothic look. “There’s no highlight, no skin showing through,” he said. The hairstylist Serge Normant also was inspired by the designer: “The way L’Wren wears things, it doesn’t look overly done. The girls aren’t supposed to look like her, but I wanted that easiness.” Hair was brushed into a deep side part with volume added through the crown of the head for a “just woke up” look, which Normant set with products from his new namesake product line. The manicurist Yuna Park filled out the look with one coat of a gold-flecked black nail polish from Lancome called Noir 29, available this fall. You know you love it. XOXO.

headline.main: Backstage Beauty | L’Wren Scott

docs.lead_paragraph: One of the most urgent and certainly among the most beautifully shot documentaries to hit the big screen in recent memory, “The Last Lions” isn’t just another cute and fuzzy encounter session with a different species. It’s a pulse-quickening, tear-duct milking and outrageously dramatized story about the threats — wildfires, chomping teeth, stampeding hooves and, worst of all, unseen humans — that face a female lion trying to protect her cubs. Here, single motherhood doesn’t mean juggling family, work and PTA meetings: it means parking the tots in the bushes and then trying to take down a water buffalo the size of a jeep.

docs.abstract: Joyce Carol Oates’s memoir of her husband’s death is more painfully self-revelatory than anything she dared produce as a fiction writer or critic.
docs.snippet: Joyce Carol Oates’s memoir of her husband’s death is more painfully self-revelatory than anything she dared produce as a fiction writer or critic.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Writing up a storm, eh, Joyce?” Shortly after the sudden death of Joyce Carol Oates’s husband, Raymond Smith, in February 2008, an acquaintance put that familiar question to her. A closer friend was sure that words were tumbling forth, too. “Knowing how you write,” the friend said in a condolence note, “you may already be completing the first of many novels that will help you explore what you’ve been experiencing.” Oates felt herself “shaking with cold, with a kind of choked fury.” The Wonder Woman of American Letters, as she learned an exhibitor of her vast array of books had christened her, could not compose even a thank-you note. “Yes it’s true that I used to be a writer — a writer with a very mixed reputation — ‘controversial’ is the kindest term,” she imagined trying to explain at a somewhat calmer moment. “But now — I am not a writer now. I am not anything now. Legally I am a ‘widow’ — that is the box I must check. But beyond that — I am not sure that I ­exist.”

headline.main: Joyce Carol Oates’s Widow’s Lament
headline.print_headline: What Remains

docs.lead_paragraph: When we speak of literary taste, we may imagine we refer to preferences regarding subject matter, genre, form and the varieties of narrative prowess. But much of what taste in reading boils down to is less conducive to objective analysis, less neatly parceled into scholarly-sounding brackets. Simply, it’s the extent to which we take pleasure in the company of the author — or rather, a facsimile thereof, a phantom version composed of and subsisting on words alone.

docs.snippet: A nice little school gets mentioned in the same breath as Harvard, Princeton and Yale by whipping them on the squash court, over and over again.
docs.lead_paragraph: One day in 1996, Trinity College’s new president, Evan Dobelle, called the men’s squash coach into his office. Dobelle was an unconventional hire. He didn’t complete his bachelor’s degree until he was 39, working in politics — mayor of Pittsfield, Mass., aide to President Carter, treasurer of the Democratic National Committee — then running first one, then another community college. But Trinity was a troubled institution, and the trustees weren’t looking for another tweedy scholar. Enrollment was down even as the liberal-arts school was accepting 65 percent of all applicants — a striking contrast to its rivals Amherst and Williams, which typically admit fewer than 20 percent of their applicant pools. The biggest problem was Trinity’s immediate surroundings, the crime-­ridden, blighted neighborhood of Frog Hollow in Hartford. So Dobelle started an ambitious $225 million public-private urban-renewal project to improve the area — including the construction of three schools and a performing-arts center — without pushing its residents out. Then he turned to the college’s sports programs, wondering if there might not be a quicker way to improve Trinity’s brand.

headline.main: Squashing the Ivies

docs.abstract: A Little Stockholm right here in New York.
docs.snippet: A Little Stockholm right here in New York.
docs.lead_paragraph: Our love for all things Swedish knows no bounds. Would that we could have a Little Stockholm right here in New York, a neighborhood where’d snap up our favorite Scandanavian duds (and meatballs). So imagine our excitement when we found out that the Swedish label Our Legacy has built a temporary corner shop at Odin that will be open throughout spring. It’s the largest selection of Our Legacy wares outside of Sweden, including a sizable pick from their latest collection, “Observations.” A one-stop spot for an entire wardrobe, the store sells eminently wearable pieces — go-anywhere tees, soft plaid Oxfords, lightly structured blazers, no-fuss pants — designed to be layered and assembled into an outfit as easily as an Ikea bookcase.

docs.snippet: There’s a secret to delicious gluhwein: don’t cook it.
docs.lead_paragraph: I’ve never had a particularly great rapport with mulled wine, that staple of ski slopes and Christmas markets throughout Northern Europe. In theory it should be a tremendously restorative, literally heartwarming (one tries to avoid the reference to Gemütlichkeit) tonic from the alpine quiver, carried to table preferably by a St. Bernard. In reality, however, I couldn’t count how many frankly off-putting mulled wines I’ve choked down slopeside over the years: harsh reds gussied up with a load of sugar and overwhelming spices to cover their unpalatable edge, then cooked, which only intensifies the jangle. Nein, danke.

docs.abstract: An unexpected rash, an unexpected cause.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Whoa! That is definitely not poison oak,” Dr. Walter Larsen blurted as he entered the exam room in his Portland, Ore., office. The patient smiled ruefully. “I told you,” she said to the doctor. The 56-year-old woman had seen Larsen that Tuesday, two days earlier. Then she was concerned; now she was scared. She looked down at her hands and arms. Her fair skin was nearly hidden by vicious-looking streaks of red. “And it’s everywhere.” She lowered the office gown to reveal scarlet lines crisscrossing up her arms, across her neck, down her back, chest and abdomen. Larsen leaned in close to get a better look at the patient’s red-streaked skin. He didn’t know what this rash was, but it sure had become a lot uglier in just a couple of days.

docs.abstract: The Lonely Island has reinvented the novelty song for the digital age.
docs.snippet: The Lonely Island has reinvented the novelty song for the digital age.
docs.lead_paragraph: The novelty song used to be popular, but it has never, ever been cool. Whether it was Allan Sherman making his 1963 hit “Hello Mudduh! Hello Fadduh!” or Weird Al Yankovic parodying Michael Jackson with “Eat It” in 1984, the comedian who made singalong spoofs was like the hip stand-up comic’s embarrassing country cousin. There were exceptions, of course, like the cerebral, political Tom Lehrer — but let’s just say that, in general, Lenny Bruce and George Carlin did not sing. The novelty song was an outlet for nerds, morning-show shock jocks and the kind of guys who put the word “weird” in front of their names. This might help explain why the era of the novelty song seemed to end right around the time that hip-hop came of age: the greatness of Weird Al’s “Straight Outta Lynwood” notwithstanding, the average funny-song singer was not cut out to spoof N.W.A.

docs.abstract: Three new collections illuminate the life and work of Elizabeth Bishop, including her time as a poet for The New Yorker.
docs.snippet: Three new collections illuminate the life and work of Elizabeth Bishop, including her time as a poet for The New Yorker.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the decades since her death in 1979, Elizabeth Bishop has been recognized as an American original, as much ours and not ours as Whitman, Dickinson and that transplanted Yankee Robert Frost. A reader’s appetite for the lives of beloved poets can be hard to satisfy. Their mortgages are subject to scholarly study, their medical records sold in shadowy alleys, their childhood friends dunned to offer up nuggets of gossip. We would read their shopping lists if we could — such things make them more human, and therefore slightly inhuman, since how is it possible that the authors of “Leaves of Grass” or “Because I Could Not Stop for Death” or “North of Boston” could have needed new stockings, and hair oil, and cornflakes?

docs.snippet: Visual histories of fanzines, horror magazines and banned comics, and of the Italian shelter magazine Abitare.
docs.lead_paragraph: I recently subscribed to a well-known magazine that offers an interactive digital edition for my iPad. I was utterly disappointed. As a magazine geek for many dec­ades, I looked forward to complaining about how nothing is better than turning real pages, smelling real ink and caressing real paper. But sadly, I have finally come to recognize that after all that turning, smelling and caressing, what remains are piles of old magazines collecting dust. The new digital version may seem less substantial, but it doesn’t have those annoying loose subscription cards or peel-and-sniff perfume ads that induce headaches (and depressing sensory memories). What’s more, I don’t have to tie up digital magazines for disposal on recycling day. So I canceled all but one print subscription, and now I get my periodical enjoyment from an iPad. Which is actually why I am pleased to see new books devoted to printed magazines. Just in case the end of print comes tomorrow, we’ll never forget what we had.

docs.snippet: Bettany Hughes examines the life and death of Socrates, and the city that nurtured and killed him.
docs.lead_paragraph: The problem with writing a biography of Socrates, as Bettany Hughes merrily admits, is that he’s a “doughnut subject”: a rich and tasty topic with a big hole right in the middle where the main character should be. Despite his fame and his insistence on an examined life, Socrates never wrote anything, and our knowledge of him comes mainly from three contemporaries — his devoted pupils Plato and Xenophon, and the parodist Aristophanes — each of whom had his own agenda. He produced no great answers, only great questions, and the most enduring image we have of his life is his leaving of it, as the title of this book suggests.

docs.snippet: An acerbic comic novel about an old divorced couple gradually finding a spark of reconnection.
docs.lead_paragraph: In a survey of unhappy families, you’d be hard pressed to find one quite so spectacularly savage as the Goodyews of Kent. In Louise Dean’s darkly comic new novel, “The Old Romantic,” Nick Goodyew, an English solicitor specializing in divorce, hasn’t seen his father, Ken, in 15 years, his mother, Pearl, in over 20 — since Nick more or less broke up the family by revealing his father’s infidelities, then escaped to the loftier world of Cambridge. When Ken gets back in touch after years of silence, it’s largely to heap abuse on his son — “Oy! Big’ead! . . . You’re nothing! You’re a stuck-up, jumped-up . . . embarrassment” — before admitting that he’ll be requiring Nick’s services in divorcing his second wife, a squat, tittering woman whose banal chatter Ken likens to a “dripping tap.”

docs.lead_paragraph: We Americans love to uproot ourselves and head out for unfamiliar territories. Our reasons, if sometimes murky, are also manifold: a fear of what’s brewing at home or the ache for an ideal that virgin land might help realize. We want riches. We thrill at jumping into the uncertain void. “West of Here,” Jonathan Evison’s broad-spectrum new novel, plays host, gleefully and mischievously, to all of the above. More than a dozen central characters willfully flip their lives upside down and inside out, eyes on the horizon.

docs.lead_paragraph: Virginia Heffernan’s opinion piece offered at best a misleading and unsubstantiated characterization of WebMD. WebMD has earned the trust of millions of consumers by providing objective and relevant health information that is written by a staff of professional journalists and board-certified physicians. Our award-winning content undergoes a rigorous medical-review process to ensure that it is credible and accurate. We always make a clear distinction between our own content and that of our advertisers. Heffernan asserts that MayoClinic.com is somehow more credible because it is owned by a nonprofit clinic, when in fact, as Heffernan acknowledges, it operates a commercial site that accepts advertising just as WebMD does. We would have also expected The Times to disclose its ownership of the advertising-supported health site on About.com, which competes with WebMD.

docs.lead_paragraph: Emily Bazelon’s article illustrates the need to reform a system in which expert medical witnesses who may have conflicts of interest argue complex cases to a lay jury. These expert witnesses are paid lucratively, can legally opine on anything outside their field and rarely face repercussions for incorrect testimony. To remove conflict of interest, the courts should seek interpretation of M.R.I.’s and other test results from multiple independent court-employed neuroradiologists who don’t have knowledge of or involvement with the case.

docs.lead_paragraph: LATE winter is traditionally a time to celebrate great acting, as the most distinguished performances of the previous year parade before us on their long march to the Oscars. At the moment, accordingly, those of us with deadlines and airtime to fill are busy trumpeting the artistry of Colin Firth and Annette Bening, Natalie Portman and Christian Bale. But meanwhile, in the real world of day-to-day moviegoing, there are screens and seats to be filled, and genre movies  horror, action, romantic comedy, kiddie adventure  flood the multiplexes, forgoing the Academy’s consideration and hoping for a bit of yours. Many of these movies take part in another, less-heralded seasonal ritual: the spectacle of great actors appearing in bad movies.
