docs.abstract: In his latest video project, Aitken sits with artists such as Jack White, to discuss nothing less than the future of art itself.
docs.snippet: In his latest video project, Aitken sits with artists such as Jack White, to discuss nothing less than the future of art itself.
docs.lead_paragraph: There are certain things that creative people share in common, and lately a chat with the artist Doug Aitken seems to be one of them. Aitken’s 2006 book, “Broken Screen,” featured interviews with 26 artists, including Robert Altman and Rem Koolhaas. Now, with his latest video project, “Patterns & Repetition,” the artist sits down with a new cast in an attempt to put the pieces of the creative puzzle back together again. Each week, The Moment will feature a different segment: Mike Kelley talking about the Motor City; Jacques Herzog on instinct and architecture; Jack White (above) imagining Michelangelo as a modern-day blogger. But don’t be fooled by the coffee mugs and the California sunshine. Aitken doesn’t do anything casually. The subtext of the conversations is nothing less than the future of art itself.

headline.main: Videophiles | Doug Aitken’s Patterns & Repetition: Jack White

docs.snippet: Is Goldman the A.I.G. Villain?| In I.P.O.’s, Cheap Content Is King| Exchange Code Names
docs.lead_paragraph: Is Goldman Really to Blame? Some bloggers take issue with the view that Goldman Sachs was responsible for the 2008 collapse of the American International Group. “For me, it is difficult to see any malpractice from Goldman here. Goldman acted to protect itself, as it had every right to do. If A.I.G. did not want to have to accept Goldman’s valuations, it could have negotiated a different valuation procedure for the trades. Instead it left itself open to massive liquidity risk by agreeing to the collateral arrangements that it did. A.I.G. never considered the consequences were the underlyings to its trades to become illiquid, nor where it would find the collateral were the trades to go against them. For me that is by far the worst of the behavior seen here.” Deus Ex Macchiato

docs.abstract: This year, designers from Thakoon to Chris Benz dressed models in manly plaids.
docs.snippet: This year, designers from Thakoon to Chris Benz dressed models in manly plaids.
docs.lead_paragraph: Men’s-wear-inspired women’s wear isn’t anything revolutionary. From Diane Keaton in “Annie Hall” wearing Ralph Lauren to Cate Blanchett channeling Katharine Hepburn in “The Aviator,” dressing like the boys doesn’t have to mean androgyny. This fall plaids are designers latest nod to men’s wear — and we’re not talking suits. Thakoon’s tribal-inspired cobalt blue and cherry red checkered 18th-century red puffer jacket would be foreign to Gaelic Scots. Similarly, Rag & Bone used a mixed color palette, but also paired neo-traditional houndstooth kilts with tough biker jackets. Some were more direct: Theyskens’ Theory delivered plaids exactly how you want and expect them, a little oversized and unbuttoned, as if you threw on your boyfriend’s. Conservative looks did resurface, however — patterns woven in maroon, brown and yellow made an appearance at Chris Benz as a simple long smock dress and Altuzarra-fitted trousers. Thankfully, this is one of those brilliant trends that you always have somewhere buried in your closet. Happy hunting.

headline.main: New York Fashion Week | Plenty of Plaid

docs.abstract: How a Mississippi slave built an information network across the South.
docs.snippet: How a Mississippi slave built an information network across the South.
docs.lead_paragraph: William Webb was a typical Southerner. He was born in Georgia in the late 1840s, but like hundreds of thousands of Americans he rode the expansion of cotton westward, carried as a teenager first to Mississippi and then to Kentucky. Webb spent long days at work outdoors: driving wagons, hoeing cotton, harvesting tobacco. When he needed to raise cash, he sold homemade treats at camp meetings, those lengthy religious revivals popular among antebellum Americans. Webb started with ginger cakes, but when he realized that the Christians were not averse to something stronger, so he quickly switched to whiskey. It “paid the best,” Webb later admitted in a narrative he wrote years later.

headline.main: William Webb’s World

docs.snippet: A French court on Friday convicted the prominent commentator Éric Zemmour on charges of “provocation to racial discrimination” for televised comments.
docs.lead_paragraph: A French court on Friday convicted the prominent commentator Éric Zemmour on charges of “provocation to racial discrimination” for televised comments in which he suggested that a majority of criminals in France were “black and Arab,” and said that employers “have the right” to deny employment to those ethnic groups. Mr. Zemmour was ordered to pay over $14,000 in legal fees and damages to the five rights groups that were the plaintiffs in the case, and also received suspended fines totaling $2,700. The commentator had “gone beyond the permitted bounds of the right to freedom of speech,” the court wrote in its decision, adding that Mr. Zemmour had a particular responsibility to respect those limits as a “professional of the media and of expression.” Mr. Zemmour’s lawyer, Olivier Pardo, said his client had not yet decided if he would appeal the decision.

headline.main: France: Commentator Convicted for Inciting Racial Bias

docs.abstract: The recently deceased Ohio Theater in SoHo will not have to wait long for a resurrection.
docs.snippet: The recently deceased Ohio Theater in SoHo will not have to wait long for a resurrection.
docs.lead_paragraph: The recently deceased Ohio Theater in SoHo will not have to wait long for a resurrection. SoHo Think Tank, the company that ran the Ohio, an Off Off Broadway theater at 66 Wooster Street, for almost 20 years, will have a new home at the Archive Building at 154 Christopher Street in the West Village beginning this fall. The original Wooster Street building was sold in 2008, and the company was forced to leave two years later after failing to renegotiate the rent with the new landlord. Since then the Think Tank has been operating under the banner “Ohio Interrupted” at the 3 Legged-Dog theater in Lower Manhattan. It will produce its annual Ice Factory festival there this summer before moving in September to the new 73-seat theater, where it will reopen under a subsidized 10-year lease and a new name, Ohio West. “To be back in our own space within a year of leaving Wooster Street, and to be in the West Village, no less, is just unbelievable,” said the company’s artistic director, Robert Lyons, above. The new building is owned by Rockrose Development, which designated the theater for nonprofit use at below market rates as part of an agreement made with the city during the commercial development of the building in 1988.

headline.main: SoHo Theater Is Reborn in the West Village

docs.abstract: Liam Neeson’s stolen-identity thriller “Unknown” was a surprise No. 1 at North American theaters over the weekend.
docs.snippet: Liam Neeson’s stolen-identity thriller “Unknown” was a surprise No. 1 at North American theaters over the weekend.
docs.lead_paragraph: Liam Neeson’s stolen-identity thriller “Unknown” was a surprise No. 1 at North American theaters over the weekend, gunning past “I Am Number Four,” a science-fiction entry that represented the reconfigured debut of Steven Spielberg’s DreamWorks Studios. Made for about $30 million, “Unknown” (Dark Castle/Warner Brothers) sold an estimated $21.8 million, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles box office statistics. “I Am Number Four,” which received negative reviews, cost at least $50 million to make and was predicted by some analysts to lead the weekend box office derby, sold about $19.5 million for second place. It was the first film that DreamWorks has released since refinancing itself and breaking ties with Paramount Pictures in favor of a distribution relationship with Walt Disney Studios. “Gnomeo & Juliet” (Disney) was a strong third with $19.4 million, bringing the two-week total for the 3-D animated comedy to about $50.4 million. The Adam Sandler-Jennifer Aniston comedy “Just Go With It” (Sony Pictures Entertainment) placed fourth in its second weekend, selling an estimated $18.2 million for a new total of $60.8 million. “Big Mommas: Like Father, Like Son,” a comedy from 20th Century Fox and New Regency starring Martin Lawrence in fat-suit drag, rounded out the top five with about $17 million.

headline.main: The Thriller ‘Unknown’ Tops the Box Office

docs.snippet: The American Cinema Editors’ choice, a good predictor for the best picture Oscar, has scrambled the race as it heads into the home stretch.
docs.lead_paragraph: With less than a week to go, the pace of tea-leaf-reading – and stirring – is approaching Daytona levels. On Saturday the American Cinema Editors guild, considered a good harbinger of the best picture Oscar, announced its winners (known as the Eddies), and it was enough to cause – if we’re going to keep going with this metaphor – a tempest in a teapot. The big prize went to Angus Wall and Kirk Baxter for “The Social Network” over “The King’s Speech” (and over “Black Swan,” “The Fighter” and “Inception”). In the comedy/musical category, “Alice in Wonderland” bested “The Kids Are All Right” and several other non-Oscar contenders, and “Exit Through the Gift Shop” won for documentary – an illustration of how well-liked it is as a film. Meanwhile pundits pounced on a victory for anything other than the projected favorite, “The King’s Speech.”

headline.main: Editors Pick ‘Social Network,’ Adding Some Oscar Intrigue

docs.lead_paragraph: You’ve heard of high-tech start-ups being in “stealth mode,” meaning they’re not telling anyone what they’re up to yet. It has a glamorous aura to it, conjuring up images of a brilliant project in the works that will soon be sprung upon the world, disrupting established players and leaving everyone scrambling to catch up. All smart companies with really great innovations keep those ideas hidden away until they’re ready to release them, lest competitors steal them. Look at Apple, which has perfected the art of secretiveness, to enormous profit. You can tell people about your great idea — but only if they sign one of those nondisclosure agreements you keep in your briefcase at all times. No exceptions!

headline.main: Got a Great Idea? Tell Everyone!

docs.lead_paragraph: Are there enough categories in the Academy Awards race? Not according to Alice Rawsthorn, design columnist for The International Herald Tribune. She proposes an Oscar for the opening and closing credits and offers her own nominees for the most creative, or effective, of this movie season. Typography is important but not always paramount. Her standard is one set by Saul Bass, who worked on Hitchcock, Kubrick and Scorsese films among many others: Do the credits set the mood for the movie to come? As he said in a 1966 interview with Film Quarterly, “I saw the title as a way of conditioning the audience, so that when the film actually began, viewers would have an emotional resonance with it.”

docs.abstract: How to achieve that metallic eye effect, off the runway.
docs.snippet: How to achieve that metallic eye effect, off the runway.
docs.lead_paragraph: When it comes to makeup, the runway often resembles a glamorous laboratory, where mad scientists (a k a makeup artists) cook up otherworldly or exaggerated looks that work well in photos but rarely make it to real life. The molten silver eye at Prada’s spring show seemed exactly that — a hothouse exotic that wouldn’t survive outside a fashion show. Not so, according to Pat McGrath, who created the look and also employed silver at Valentino and Galliano. “Metallics are unique, modern and chic,” she says. “But most of all, they are completely wearable on every skin tone.” For an evening out, she suggests using Laura Mercier’s intense Foiled Eye Color in V.I.P. Silver on the lid, keeping the color centered, rather than extending up to the brow, and following with black liquid liner and mascara. For day, try Covergirl Smoky ShadowBlast in Silver Sky from the lash line to the browbone, and finish with two coats of mascara. Romy Soleimani, who created the liquid mercury look for this story, recommends a sheer wash of Make Up For Ever Aqua Cream No. 3 all over the lid and in the crease, followed by mascara. “Fill in your brow, do a beautiful pale pink lip, and you have a delicate version of the look,” she says.

headline.main: Silver Lining

docs.lead_paragraph: At first, even second glance, Eric Cantona, 44, looks as if he could be minutes away from shedding his stylish street clothes and stepping back onto the soccer field without embarrassing himself. Cantona has been named the director of soccer operations for the reborn New York Cosmos, a team that really is not a team — yet — but that hopes to become the 20th entry in Major League Soccer, perhaps as soon as the 2013 season. Cantona spoke with Jack Bell of The Times (who, as he took notes using an iPad and wireless keyboard, heard Cantona say that he felt “strange, like I’m talking to the police at the station”) about his days at Old Trafford, his exploits on the silver screen and his expectations with the Cosmos.

docs.lead_paragraph: This is the view from the American outpost at Band-e Sardeh, in Ghazni Province. To the left is a large Soviet-built reservoir. Its pale green surface, at least near the dam beneath the road, is now frozen. The dam was built by the Soviet Union in the 1960s, during the Kremlin’s long and frustrating period of Moscow-Kabul engagement. The American outpost today lies within the confines of what was once a much larger Soviet Army position astride a significant Kremlin public-works investment. Last fall, before air and water temperatures plummeted with the onset of the Afghan winter, the American soldiers here swam in the lake, no doubt just like their Soviet predecessors did.

docs.lead_paragraph: After months of insufferable rumor after insufferable rumor, Carmelo Anthony is finally set to be a Knick. But Anthony is not the only likely inbound Nugget; Chauncey Billups will take over the outgoing Raymond Felton’s job as starting point guard, and three role players – Shelden Williams, Anthony Carter and Renaldo Balkman – could help fill in minutes at the bottom of Coach Mike D’Antoni’s rotation. This is obviously a substantial deal for New York, as D’Antoni will have to integrate two major contributors on the fly while also dealing with the losses of Felton, Danilo Gallinari, Wilson Chandler  and Timofey Mozgov. docs.lead_paragraph: Mark Seliger’s collection of nudes, portraits and landscapes is just about the handsomest book of photographs to be published in a while. Every detail of “Listen,” from the quality of the binding and endpapers to the selection and reproduction of the platinum-plated prints, is a book-lover’s treat. Mr. Seliger is such a believer. And he has put together a book, with Rizzoli, that sharpens the senses for the silent and seemingly insignificant. He is well known for his portraits of actors and musicians and his fashion work for magazines, among them Vanity Fair and Italian Vogue. “Listen” displays a natural feeling for things that hover between ordinary and monumental, sad and self-renewing. You can catch his show of photographs from “Listen” at the Steven Kasher Gallery in Chelsea; it closes on Saturday. Here’s an excerpt from our recent conversation.

headline.main: Playing a Sad Song for Joy: Mark Seliger

docs.snippet: The American Folk Art Museum, which is facing serious financial problems, is nonetheless embarking an ambitious project: an exhibition of African-American self-taught and graffiti artists to take place in Venice during the Biennale there.
docs.lead_paragraph: The American Folk Art Museum, which is facing serious financial problems, is nonetheless embarking an ambitious project: an exhibition of African-American self-taught and graffiti artists to take place in Venice during the Biennale there. The exhibition will open June 1 at the Fondaco dei Tedeschi, a building owned by the Benetton Group that may ultimately become a Rem Koolhaas-designed retail and exhibition space. Benetton is offering the building to the museum for free, as well as providing advertising and art materials and holding the opening-night party. The museum’s director, Maria Ann Conelli, said that the budget for the one-month exhibition was between $300,000 and $400,000 and that the museum was reaching out to foundations and corporations for financing. Since January, the museum has been unable to make payments on the roughly $30 million it owes against its building on West 53rd Street. Last summer, it entered into a forbearance agreement with the company that insured its debt, ACA Financial Guaranty. That agreement expires on June 30. According to the most recent available financial statements, in the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2010, the museum ran a deficit from unrestricted activities of $3.6 million. Ms. Conelli said that the museum had a balanced budget for this year.

headline.main: Folk Art Museum to Show Self-Taught Black Artists in Venice

docs.abstract: A set of important murals depicting events in African-American history will be restored and sent on tour for the first time through a collaboration of Talladega College in Alabama, which owns the murals, and the High Museum of Art in Atlanta.
docs.snippet: A set of important murals depicting events in African-American history will be restored and sent on tour for the first time through a collaboration of Talladega College in Alabama, which owns the murals, and the High Museum of Art in Atlanta.
docs.lead_paragraph: A set of important murals depicting events in African-American history will be restored and sent on tour for the first time through a collaboration of Talladega College in Alabama, which owns the murals, and the High Museum of Art in Atlanta. In 1938 Talladega, one of the country’s oldest all-black colleges, commissioned Hale Aspacio Woodruff, an African-American artist who had studied with Diego Rivera, to create the murals for the lobby of its new library. Comprising six canvases, the murals depict events like the uprising on the slave ship La Amistad, scenes from the Underground Railroad and the founding of the college. At the High, the murals will be cleaned and restretched, Philip Verre, the museum’s chief operating officer, said in a phone interview. They will go on view in an exhibition opening in Atlanta on June 2, 2012, and will travel later to the Indianapolis Museum of Art. Woodruff, who taught art at New York University for more than 20 years, died in 1980. He had a retrospective at the Studio Museum in Harlem in 1979 and an exhibition at the High Museum, focused on his paintings in Atlanta, in 2004.

headline.main: Historic African American Murals to Be Restored

docs.abstract: The male counterpoint to Net-a-Porter, the high-end fashion e-tailer, is finally live after more than a little hype over the past few months.
docs.snippet: The male counterpoint to Net-a-Porter, the high-end fashion e-tailer, is finally live after more than a little hype over the past few months.
docs.lead_paragraph: Gentlemen, get out your plastic and get ready to spend till you bend: Mr. Porter, the male counterpoint to Net-a-Porter, the high-end fashion e-tailer, is finally live after more than a little hype over the past few months. Aimed at men who want to purchase clothes, accessories and other dapper goods online, Mr. Porter is a stand-alone destination, not an add-on to its sister site. “We started from scratch,” said Natalie Massenet, the founder of Net-a-Porter. “We didn’t want to simply include a men’s tab on Net-a-Porter.” Massenet hired the former British Esquire editor Jeremy Langmead and a team of experienced men’s-wear editors to tailor the editorial content (style advice, guides and portfolios of non-models like the poet Nick Laird, above) for an audience that is generally held to be more interested in connoisseurship than in passing fads. Not surprisingly, the site will carry classic establishment brands like Ralph Lauren and Dunhill as well as harder-to-find heritage labels like Lock & Co. and Swayne Adeney Brigg. Its handsome black and white packaging will ship to 170 countries, proving that for stylish men, even e-commerce is all about the details.

headline.main: The Site Makes the Man

docs.abstract: A lecture by the Nigerian author and Nobel Prize winner Wole Soyinka, readings by Wallace Shawn and Malcolm Gladwell, a debate on the prison industry, and an evening on the topic of sex led by Edmund White are among the offerings at this year’s PEN World Voices Festival of International Literature.
docs.snippet: A lecture by the Nigerian author and Nobel Prize winner Wole Soyinka, readings by Wallace Shawn and Malcolm Gladwell, a debate on the prison industry, and an evening on the topic of sex led by Edmund White are among the offerings at this year’s PE...
docs.lead_paragraph: A lecture by the Nigerian author and Nobel Prize winner Wole Soyinka, readings by Wallace Shawn and Malcolm Gladwell, a debate on the prison industry and an evening on the topic of sex led by Edmund White are among the offerings at this year’s PEN World Voices Festival of International Literature, which will take place from April 25 to May 1 in New York. Other events in the festival, which is put on by the PEN American Center, include a discussion of cultural and political conditions in China featuring the New Yorker contributor Jianying Zha; a night with the storytelling group the Moth, on the theme of “What’s Gone Wrong”; a celebration of poetry, curated by Laurie Anderson and featuring Antony and the Johnsons; and a game of telephone in which a Tibetan lama will pass along sutras down a list of 200 festival attendees, ending with Salman Rushdie, who will Tweet the result. The festival, which is being organized by the former Hungarian Cultural Center director Laszlo Jakab Orsos, will be based out of the Standard Hotel, with events taking place at the New York Public Library, Cooper Union, the 92nd Street Y and elsewhere. Mr. White’s sex event, which, according to a news release, will feature “celebrated members” of the fashion and music worlds, will take place in the Standard’s rooftop bar, Le Bain (French for “the bath”).

headline.main: PEN World Voices Festival Announces Lineup

docs.abstract: Justin Bieber, Lady Gaga, Mumford & Sons and Lady Antebellum all got big “Grammy lifts” — the typical boost in record sales after the awards show.
docs.snippet: Justin Bieber, Lady Gaga, Mumford & Sons and Lady Antebellum all got big “Grammy lifts” — the typical boost in record sales after the awards show.
docs.lead_paragraph: Justin Bieber, Lady Gaga, Mumford & Sons and Lady Antebellum all got big “Grammy lifts” — the typical boost in record sales after the awards show. But who had the biggest lift depends on how you look at the numbers. Mr. Bieber, who did not win any awards but who had a prominent performing slot at the ceremony, dominates this week’s Billboard album chart. “Never Say Never: The Remixes” (Island), the soundtrack to his new 3-D concert film, opened at No. 1 with 161,000 copies sold. But just as impressive, he has three other albums in the Top 40: “My World 2.0” is No. 8, “My Worlds Acoustic” is No. 18, and “My World,” the mini-album that was his debut, is No. 31. Billboard said Mr. Bieber was the first artist to pull off that feat since Garth Brooks in 1993. The British alt-folk band Mumford & Sons and Lady Antebellum, the country-pop trio that went home with the most Grammy awards (five, including record and song of the year), also had good runs on the album chart. Mumford & Sons’ “Sigh No More” (Glassnote) holds at No. 2 this week. Its rise to No. 2 from No. 11 last week was largely based on impulse buys made during the Grammys telecast, on which the group performed with Bob Dylan, with 133,000 sales, a 169 percent increase from the week before. Lady Antebellum’s “Need You Now” (Capitol Nashville) is No. 4, with 85,000 sales, a 205 percent gain. (No. 3 this week goes to Vol. 37 of the series “Now That’s What I Call Music!,” which sold 95,000.) In terms of digital downloads, however, Lady Gaga and Cee Lo Green came out way ahead. “Born This Way,” which Lady Gaga performed at the awards, sold 509,000 copies in its first full week on sale, bringing its total sales in the United States — in just 10 days — to 957,000. And sales of Cee Lo’s “____ You” jumped 178 percent, to 412,000.

headline.main: Bieber Dominates Billboard Chart

docs.lead_paragraph: The choreographer Paul Taylor  one of the few living artists who have made classics by which our age should be remembered  is a puzzle, and means to be. He makes works whose rhythms answer that of their music, except sometimes they carry on regardless. He makes dances that are primarily about dancing, except that in many of them he seems preoccupied by more specific subject matter. His pieces are addressed to the audience in a way that speaks of entertainment (bright, harsh or both) and yet frequently they do things that will make audiences think, “We should be entertained by that?” His company’s repertory has become so large  his latest is listed as Opus No. 133  that each year brings a major revival of at least one important work that hasn’t been seen in decades. It contains many other pieces that get revived only fleetingly before being returned to cold storage for several more seasons.

docs.snippet: International moviegoing soared in 2010, but the North American market started to show more signs of trouble.
docs.lead_paragraph: International moviegoing soared in 2010, but the North American market started to show more signs of trouble, according to an annual survey released on Wednesday by the Motion Picture Association of America. Total box office receipts for all films released around the world climbed to $31.8 billion, an 8 percent increase over 2009. But overseas ticket sales contributed all of the increase, as sales in North America were flat for a second year, at $10.6 billion, despite a boom in sales of higher-priced 3-D tickets. “The Chinese box office market is just going gangbusters,” said Bob Pisano, president and interim chief executive of the movie association. The association does not report overseas attendance figures; admissions in North America fell 5 percent, to 1.34 billion. In a development that Mr. Pisano called “not so encouraging” the number of North American admissions per capita fell to 4.1, the lowest level since 1993, from 4.3 in 2009. Mr. Pisano said he was unsure of the reason, but added, “We’ve got to get more Americans and Canadians back to the movie theaters.”

headline.main: Moviegoing Leaps, Except in North America

docs.abstract: Why does being out of a job leave you with so little time for the kids?
docs.snippet: Why does being out of a job leave you with so little time for the kids?
docs.lead_paragraph: Since losing my job I’ve struggled with countless questions for which I have no suitable response: Is it healthy for my family to subsist on a diet entirely of packaged ramen, canned beans and grocery-store samples, and if so, must it be certified organic? Does baby really need a new pair of shoes? If I’m so smart how come I’m so broke? The worst question, though, and the one most likely to induce paroxysms of guilt, irritation and half-joking existential despair, is one that seems so simple to answer, but has proven the most vexing: if I’m not working, why don’t I have more time? Shouldn’t a jobless fellow like myself be free to relax, clean house, run errands for my fiancée Tomoko and, most important, spend time with my children, J.P., 4-years-old, and Ellie, the baby?

headline.main: Out of Work, Out of Time

docs.lead_paragraph: Histories of mid-19th century America tend to separate its two most important threads: a war over slavery engulfs the East, while mineral rushes transform the West. docs.abstract: For the street artist known only as JR, the world is a canvas.
docs.snippet: For the street artist known only as JR, the world is a canvas.
docs.lead_paragraph: In a Paris suburb in October 2005, two teenagers of African descent were running away from the police and tried to hide inside a power substation. They were electrocuted instantly. The violence that broke out in protest of police harassment soon spread to neighboring communities and eventually to housing projects across the whole of France. When the media came to document the events in Clichy-sous-Bois, they were met with an additional, unexpected kind of confrontation: behind one of the countless cars in flames was a black-and-white photograph that was pasted onto the side of an apartment building some time before and took up its entire width. From its center, surrounded by a group of boys striking aggressive poses, a black man several times larger than life stared out, pointing with what appeared at first to be a shotgun. On closer inspection, it was a video camera. Get out, he seemed to be saying, we’re recording this too, and we’ll tell the story the way we see it.

headline.main: Supercolossal Street Art

docs.abstract: Mr. Hopkins, the star of “The Remains of the Day” and “The Silence of the Lambs,” will appear in a series of concerts in which the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra will perform music that he composed.
docs.snippet: Mr. Hopkins, the star of “The Remains of the Day” and “The Silence of the Lambs,” will appear in a series of concerts in which the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra will perform music that he composed.
docs.lead_paragraph: With some tours, you wonder what songs will appear on the set list; for this one, we wonder what they’ll serve at the concession stands. Anthony Hopkins, who has variously cooked up the liver of a census taker and the brain matter of Ray Liotta in his onscreen capacity as Dr. Hannibal Lecter, plans to take on more digestible material in a series of concerts featuring his own musical compositions. BBC News reported that Mr. Hopkins will participate in the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra’s summer tour of Britain, on which the orchestra will perform the original scores he created for his films “August” and “Slipstream,” as well as a new work by the actor. The orchestra, conducted by Michael Seal, will also play selections from the scores of Mr. Hopkins’s best-known films, including “The Remains of the Day” and “The Silence of the Lambs,” and Mr. Hopkins will discuss his music and creative process (and who knows, maybe even favorite recipes) with Tommy Pearson, a producer of the concerts. There was no immediate announcement if the concert series might come to the United States or if Mr. Hopkins might take a brief detour to the Bahamas to have an old friend for dinner.

headline.main: An Appetizing Proposition: Anthony Hopkins Takes His Music on Tour

docs.abstract: Gabrielle Hamilton’s brilliantly written new memoir, “Blood, Bones & Butter,” is rhapsodic about food, but it’s not just for foodies.
docs.snippet: Gabrielle Hamilton’s brilliantly written new memoir, “Blood, Bones & Butter,” is rhapsodic about food, but it’s not just for foodies.
docs.lead_paragraph: When Gabrielle Hamilton was a child, growing up in Pennsylvania, her family gave an annual party that was legendary in its small town  a spring lamb roast for almost 200 people, who came from as far away as New York City: former ballet dancer friends of her mother’s and artist friends of her father’s, along with local friends and neighbors, who all gathered in the meadow behind their house to feast on lamb and asparagus vinaigrette and shortcake. In preparation Gabrielle and her sister and brothers would fill dozens of brown paper lunch bags with sand and candles and set them along the stream’s edge under the weeping willows to light everyone’s way, and juice up glow-in-the-dark Frisbees in the car headlights, so they could send those “glowing greenish discs arcing through the jet black night.”

docs.abstract: Mr. Jones will play Arthur Hockstader, a Truman-esque chief executive deciding between endorsing potential presidential nominees William Russell and Joe Cantwell.
docs.snippet: Mr. Jones will play Arthur Hockstader, a Truman-esque chief executive deciding between endorsing potential presidential nominees William Russell and Joe Cantwell.
docs.lead_paragraph: When his time behind the wheel at “Driving Miss Daisy” comes to an end, James Earl Jones need not resort to reciting Justin Bieber lyrics for fun and profit (unless he wants to), as his next term of office on Broadway has been decided: Mr. Jones, a Tony Award winner for “Fences” and “The Great White Hope,” will next portray a former United States president in the revival of “Gore Vidal’s The Best Man,” a political play scheduled for spring of next year. Press representatives for the revival said on Thursday that Mr. Jones will play Arthur Hockstader, a Truman-esque chief executive deciding between endorsing the potential presidential nominees William Russell and Joe Cantwell. When “The Best Man” was first presented on Broadway in 1960 (and made into a film in 1964), Russell was perceived as an analogue for Adlai Stevenson and Cantwell as an amalgam of John F. Kennedy and Richard M. Nixon; a 2000 Broadway revival, starring Charles Durning as Hockstader, Spalding Gray as Russell and Chris Noth as Cantwell, seemed to have its eye on the real-life contest between Al Gore and George W. Bush. Michael Wilson (“The Orphans’ Home Cycle”) will direct the 2012 production, though its producers have not yet announced their nominees to play Russell and Cantwell.

headline.main: James Earl Jones Elected for Broadway Revival of ‘Gore Vidal’s The Best Man’

docs.lead_paragraph: FOR over half a century, Angelinos have flocked to this secluded corner of California’s Sierra Nevada mountains. It’s easy to see why. Despite the 8,000-foot altitude, Mammoth Lakes’ sprawl of splashy condos and strip malls has a distinct Los Angeles feel. But the surrounding frozen lakes and granite peaks, immortalized by the photographer Ansel Adams, are decidedly un-Los Angeles, and can hold their own with any landscape in Colorado or Canada. And with expanded daily flights from the San Francisco Bay area and Los Angeles, not to mention a flurry of new après-ski offerings, Mammoth is hoping to draw skiers from beyond the Golden State.

docs.snippet: The founding president of the Seaport Museum New York, which in recent weeks lost a third of its trustees and furloughed half its staff, has called for the resignation of the museum’s current president, Mary Pelzer, and its chairman, Frank J. Scia...
docs.lead_paragraph: 3:54 p.m. | Updated The founding president of the Seaport Museum New York, which in recent weeks lost a third of its trustees and furloughed half its staff, has called for the resignation of the museum’s current president, Mary Pelzer, and its chairman, Frank J. Sciame. In a letter to Ms. Pelzer that he shared with The New York Times, the former president, Peter Stanford, said that the museum needed new leadership to survive. He wrote that Ms. Pelzer’s and Mr. Sciame’s credibility had been damaged by “concealment” of its financial problems, and that the “overall direction of the Seaport Museum has been neglectful of its principal physical asset,” its historic ships. Mr. Sciame, a real estate developer, has lent the museum $3 million in the last year to cover operating expenses. “Mr. Sciame and Ms. Pelzer are extremely surprised and deeply disappointed by these inaccurate comments,” said Adam Pockriss of Rubenstein Communications and a spokesman for the museum. Neither Ms. Pelzer nor Mr. Sciame returned phone calls.

docs.abstract: State legislation that would have forced the University of Iowa to sell Jackson Pollock’s “Mural” — an 8-by-20-foot painting valued at more than $100 million — to raise money for the school has been dropped.
docs.snippet: State legislation that would have forced the University of Iowa to sell Jackson Pollock’s “Mural” — an 8-by-20-foot painting valued at more than $100 million — to raise money for the school has been dropped.
docs.lead_paragraph: State legislation that would have forced the University of Iowa to sell “Mural” — an 8-by-20-foot painting by Jackson Pollock valued at more than $100 million — to raise money for the school has been dropped, The Des Moines Register reported. State Representative Scott Raecker introduced the bill this month as a way to create an endowment to pay for as many as 1,000 full student scholarships a year, but the proposal drew widespread criticism. David Miles, the president of the Board of Regents, State of Iowa, described the bill as “a profoundly bad idea,” one that was examined by the board in 2008 and “determined to be not in the best interests of the University of Iowa or the state.” Mr. Raecker told the student newspaper The Daily Iowan that he still believed the painting should be sold but said that the issue had become “so polarized that reaching consensus is unlikely.” “I’m a firm believer in the legislative process,” he added, “and further discussion of the sale of the Pollock painting will not be moved forward in the legislature this year.”

headline.main: Bill Requiring the University of Iowa to Relinquish Pollock’s ‘Mural’ Is Dropped

docs.abstract: The Neue Galerie’s show “Vienna 1900: Style and Identity” is a shifting kaleidoscope of paintings, drawings, architectural models and plans, posters, furniture and more.
docs.snippet: The Neue Galerie’s show “Vienna 1900: Style and Identity” is a shifting kaleidoscope of paintings, drawings, architectural models and plans, posters, furniture and more.
docs.lead_paragraph: There’s no modernism like Viennese modernism, that amazingly fraught, conflicted efflorescence of art and thought that flared up around the turn of the 20th century. As the Austro-Hungarian Empire sank into paralysis in the decades before World War I, Freud discovered the unconscious lurking, unsurprisingly, behind the city’s repressive social codes. Otto Wagner and Adolf Loos designed buildings that rejected the historicist wedding-cake facades of the Ringstrasse. Arnold Schoenberg pursued atonal music in the perfumed wake of the Viennese waltz; and Gustav Klimt painted beautiful women surrounded by mosaic patterns straight out of Byzantium.

docs.lead_paragraph: The remaining contestants on “American Idol” performed songs from the Beatles catalog on Wednesday as the judges named 5 of the top 24 to advance. The Fox reality competition easily dominated the night’s ratings over all. According to Nielsen’s estimates, an average of 22.6 million viewers tuned in to the episode from 8 to 10 p.m. CBS’s “Criminal Minds,” with its 13.4 million viewers at 9, came closest to matching the audience for “Idol,” as CBS claimed second place, earning solid results the rest of the night for “Survivor: Redemption Island” at 8 (11.2 million) and “Criminal Minds: Suspect Behavior” at 10 (9.9 million). ABC ranked third with its comedy lineup from 8 to 10, including “Modern Family” (13.3 million) and “Mr. Sunshine” (6.5 million) in the 9 p.m. hour. NBC finished fourth with “Minute to Win It” from 8 to 10 (4.1 million), followed by “Law & Order: SVU” at 10 (8 million).

docs.abstract: “In the atmosphere of a possible murder inquiry (Emily Bazelon, Feb. 6), it may be almost impossible to establish the unvarnished truth.”
docs.snippet: “In the atmosphere of a possible murder inquiry (Emily Bazelon, Feb. 6), it may be almost impossible to establish the unvarnished truth.”
docs.lead_paragraph: In the atmosphere of a possible murder inquiry (Emily Bazelon, Feb. 6), it may be almost impossible to establish the unvarnished truth. Even so, as noted in my 1971 report, “Infantile Subdural Haematoma and Its Relationship to Whiplash Injuries,” because shaking was regarded as an acceptable form of correction in the north of England (where I practiced), the police were only involved when there were other injuries. Forty years on, our standards are higher: I have watched with fascination how medical opinion has changed from denial to admission that infant abuse could and did happen there. As the lawyers say, “Cases are decided not on the truth but on the evidence.” With no fear of prosecution, my patients’ caregivers had no motive to lie. I stand by the conclusions of my 1971 paper — that there are occasions when violent shaking can cause severe or even fatal brain damage.

docs.lead_paragraph: On television series like “Buffy” and “Dollhouse,” Eliza Dushku was perfectly comfortable holding her own against tough guys, and maybe throwing a punch or two when the situation required it. So her next role is a bit of a departure, and not only because she isn’t called upon to swing her fists. In the boxing video game Fight Night Champion, which EA Sports will release for the Xbox 360 and PlayStation3 consoles on Tuesday, Ms. Dushku plays the daughter of an unscrupulous fight promoter, and finds herself drawn into an intrigue involving her father and an up-and-coming boxer (played by the actor and athlete LaMonica Garrett). The story, which is told in movie-style sequences that unfold between the game’s playable boxing matches, is written by Will Rokos, an Academy Award-nominated writer and producer of “Monster’s Ball,” and represents the latest effort to bridge the worlds of gaming and cinema. These sequences (which were created using 3-D motion-capture technology) also allowed Ms. Dushku to play a character who was very much herself and yet as unearthly as anything seen on a Joss Whedon show.

headline.main: The Lady Is a Champ: Eliza Dushku Goes a Few Rounds With Fight Night Champion

docs.abstract: Andre Dubus III recalls his upbringing in a Massachusetts mill town, and the tormentors he and his siblings had to fight through.
docs.snippet: Andre Dubus III recalls his upbringing in a Massachusetts mill town, and the tormentors he and his siblings had to fight through.
docs.lead_paragraph: One Saturday night in the mid-’70s, I stood on the deck of a shabby duplex watching my teenage boyfriend — a character who could have walked out of the pages of Andre Dubus III’s powerful new memoir, “Townie” — beat another boy senseless in the parking lot below. Under the yellowish dusk-to-dawn lights, I could see my boyfriend’s blond sideburns, denim jacket and dingo boots, and I could see him punch the boy in the stomach until he crumpled to the ground, then kick him over and over until his nose and lips were split and bleeding. In “Townie,” which details Dubus’s 1970s coming-of-age in the poor mill towns of Massachusetts, there are none of the usual signifiers of today’s ’70s Nostalgia Industrial Complex, no peace-sign key chains or smiley-face T-shirts, none of the goofy stoners and ditsy girls in tube tops that American television viewers have become accustomed to on “That ’70s Show.” Instead, Dubus writes about “the apartments” where his older sister buys drugs, two rows of three-story buildings surrounded by packed dirt worn smooth, a Dumpster in back always filled with dirty diapers, used condoms and pizza boxes. He writes about an early manifestation of “Fight Club” culture at his school, where, whenever there is a fight, boys and girls rush to one spot “like they were being pulled there by the air itself. . . . Kids were yelling: ‘Kill him! Kill him!’ ”

docs.lead_paragraph: Solomon VOLKOV loves his czars. And in “Romanov Riches” he pays homage to them as patrons of the arts and apostles of power, sweeping the reader across 300 years of Russian history from the accession of Czar Mikhail in 1613 to the violent collapse of the imperial world in 1917. docs.snippet: A history of how three African-American families of mixed ancestry stopped being black.
docs.lead_paragraph: Racial passing is one of America’s deeply hidden traditions, a largely unacknowledged and unstudied aspect of national life. Historically, African-Americans with identifiably dark skin have had only two choices when confronting racial discrimination and oppression: either they could try to ease their burden through accommodation, making the best of a bad situation, or they could engage in protest and active resistance. The situation was often quite different, however, for light-skinned African-Americans of mixed parentage. For them, there was a tempting third option of trying to pass as white.

docs.lead_paragraph: An indelible scene from the life of Alexander the Great finds the ­prodigious warrior-king — just 25 years old in 330 B.C. — and his conquering army on a stretch of R&R at Persepolis, one of Persia’s great capitals, now marked out for plunder. During a drunken revel characteristic of the rough Macedonian court, an Athenian woman named Thais, the mistress of one of the high officers present, made a startling suggestion. It would be a fine thing, she said, if with her own hands and with Alexander looking on, she set fire to the palace built by King Xerxes, who a century and a half earlier had reduced her home city to ashes, “that it might be recorded to posterity that the women who followed Alexander had taken a severer revenge on the Persians for the sufferings and affronts of Greece, than all the famed commanders had been able to do by sea or land.”

docs.abstract: A historian of African-American entertainment seeks to rehabilitate the image of the pioneering actress and singer Ethel Waters.
docs.snippet: A historian of African-American entertainment seeks to rehabilitate the image of the pioneering actress and singer Ethel Waters.
docs.lead_paragraph: Like Eddie (Rochester) Anderson in “Cabin in the Sky,” the 1943 movie-musical parable of temptation, most Americans seem constitutionally predisposed to choose Lena Horne over Ethel Waters — that is, to prefer a model of classical beauty, sex appeal, excitement and youth to a symbol of matronly stolidity, virtue and middle-age languor. Anderson comes around to Waters, of course, when a team of celestial Simon Cowells repackages her to show that the old lady still has loads of talent, vigor and carnality in reserve. Nearly 70 years later, American culture has grown so absorbed with beauty and youthfulness that the film’s vindication of ability over appearance, depth and experience over novelty and thrills, seems even more wishfully fantastical than it was in 1943. Meanwhile, the movie’s top-billed star, Ethel Waters, has been nearly forgotten by all but enthusiasts of music and movie history.

docs.abstract: A young girl is swept up by the intrigue of the sultan’s court in this novel of the late Ottoman Empire.
docs.snippet: A young girl is swept up by the intrigue of the sultan’s court in this novel of the late Ottoman Empire.
docs.lead_paragraph: The promising opening chapters of Michael David Lukas’s first novel, “The Oracle of Stamboul,” have many of the appealing features of a fairy tale. A girl of unusual gifts is born in fulfillment of a prophecy, and after her mother dies giving birth, she is raised by a loving but weak-willed father and an oppressive stepmother, while a mysterious flock of birds follows her wherever she goes. But the girl, Eleonora Cohen, is also a Jew born into a specific historical context — the Ottoman Empire in the late-19th century — and on the day of her birth in 1877, her hometown, the Romanian port of Constanta on the Black Sea, is sacked by the Russian cavalry. This juxtaposition of fable and brute history tells us right from the start that we’re in the realm of magic realism, and the story’s tension, or lack thereof, between magic and realism is an indication of both the ambition and the shortcomings of this ultimately frustrating novel.

When a beefy thug on a pier in Cyprus dismisses him with an ostentatious yawn, Wells quickly takes him to task, dumping him into Zygi's oily harbor. docs.lead_paragraph: One of literature’s most seductive questions was asked by the Hungarian novelist Sandor Marai in “Embers,” his exquisite novel of friendship and betrayal, published in Budapest in 1942, but not translated into English until 2001, 12 years after his death. “Do you want it to be the way it used to be?” a woman asks a man. “Yes,” he responds.“Exactly the same. The way it was last time.” This exchange occurs not between lovers but between a 91-year-old servant and the 75-year-old general she nursed as a baby, in whose household she has remained. The general wants her to set up the dining room just as it looked at his life’s most critical juncture, 41 years earlier, when the closest, most sacred friendship of his youth came to an end.

docs.lead_paragraph: The would-be foreign policy prodigy Parag Khanna made a splash with his first book, “The Second World,” in 2008, by announcing with great fanfare — including a lengthy adaptation in The New York Times Magazine — what everyone already knew: that the international order was changing. The book was Khanna’s version of the fall of the West and the rise of the rest. Having described this grave new world, Khanna now wants to tell us how to run it. The result is another easy, breezy book that dispenses platitudes as though they were original insights and in the process fails to examine their actual significance.

docs.snippet: Jonas Hassen Khemiri’s novel is told in two voices, a generation and the distance from Tunisia to Sweden separating them.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Does anyone at all understand anything about a story that is not their own?” asks Kadir, one of the primary characters in Jonas Hassen Khemiri’s “Montecore: The Silence of the Tiger.” It’s an apt question in any novel, but particularly so in this one, which is told in two voices, a generation and the distance (literal, social, linguistic) from Tunisia to Sweden separating them. Khemiri offers familiar if not simple emotional territory, a story about a son and his estranged father — complicated by questions of culture and language, racism and violence, metafiction and postmodernity, formal conceit and constraint.

docs.abstract: Susan Jacoby challenges the optimistic marketing that has made old age seem pleasant and carefree.
docs.snippet: Susan Jacoby challenges the optimistic marketing that has made old age seem pleasant and carefree.
docs.lead_paragraph: Susan Jacoby has long made it her project to uncover ill-formed, cynical “junk thought” and administer a cold dose of reason and logic against it. But Jacoby is no Mr. Spock. Her rationalism is delivered in an angry barrage peppered with enthusiastically snide asides. In previous books, including “The Age of American Unreason” and “Freethinkers,” her targets have been right-leaning religionists, social Darwinists, and the paucity of reason in a generation that stares too much at glowing screens and too little at learned books. In her latest jeremiad, “Never Say Die,” she fights to slay the conspiracies of ignorance and greed that she believes conceal a single, and indeed irrefutable, truth: extreme old age can be nasty, brutish and long.

docs.lead_paragraph: A  year ago, an injury left me unable to sit. For months, I could choose only between standing and lying on my back. In the past, sick days had bought me time to read, novels anesthetizing every ill. But now, with no lap to rest a book on, books became unwieldy. Tables were too high when I lay down, too low when I stood up. Flat on the floor, I tired of propping a paperback above my head. docs.abstract: Libyan naval ships are caught in a bind: they don’t want to bombard civilians, and they don’t dare flee. Let’s help them.
docs.snippet: Libyan naval ships are caught in a bind: they don’t want to bombard civilians, and they don’t dare flee. Let’s help them.
docs.lead_paragraph: CAIRO — I’ve been on the phone today again with people in the Tripoli area in Libya, and I had an inquiry that goes to the heart of the need for NATO, the United States and Europe to move more forcefully. Several Libyan navy ships were ordered to bombard the city of Benghazi, which has been liberated by rebels. The ships’ officers don’t want to do that and don’t like Qaddafi, and they’re also fearful that if they attack Benghazi they’ll be attacked right back by shore batteries. They would like to make a run for Malta and defect, but they fear that the Libyan air force is watching them and will bomb them if they head in that direction. And the commanding officers also aren’t entirely sure who on board is trustworthy and who isn’t. They’re in a bind.

headline.main: Let’s Assure Free Passage From Libya

docs.lead_paragraph: “American Idol” filled out the rest of its slate of 24 semifinalists on Thursday as the latest two-hour installment of the singing competition topped the ratings with 21.6 million viewers, according to Nielsen’s estimates, up nearly 20 percent versus the comparable night a year ago. Fox easily led the night ahead of its network competitors, while CBS placed second, aided by solid results for “CSI” at 9 (12.5 million) and “The Mentalist” at 10 (14.7 million). At 8 and 8:30, CBS broadcast “The Big Bang Theory” (12.5 million) and “Rules of Engagement” (9.6 million). In third place, ABC posted modest ratings for “Wipeout” (7.1 million), “Grey’s Anatomy” (9.1 million) and “Private Practice” (6.7 million). NBC was fourth with low ratings for its comedy line-up, earning its most viewers at 9 for “The Office” (6.2 million).

docs.lead_paragraph: The United States economy can’t seem to catch a break. On Friday, the federal government revised its calculation of fourth-quarter growth to 2.8 percent from 3.2 percent. In the Weekend Business podcast, Catherine Rampell explains why: the turmoil in the Middle East has sent oil prices soaring. Investors fear that the unrest will spread to other countries, further disrupting production. In the United States, major cutbacks by state and local governments and threats of federal cutbacks are throwing more workers into the unemployment pool. Taken together, the uncertainty means businesses are unlikely to invest, let alone hire more workers.

docs.snippet: As a first-time nominee, Jacki Weaver had no problem admitting that she really, really wanted to win, and sharing details of her acceptance speech strategy.
docs.lead_paragraph: LOS ANGELES— Oscar loves a Cinderella story, and this year one of the best has belonged to Jacki Weaver. A veteran Australian stage actress, Ms. Weaver hadn’t been in a movie in a dozen years and was unknown in the U.S. until she starred in “Animal Kingdom,” the Australian indie crime drama from a first-time filmmaker that earned her a best supporting actress nomination. She has been a petite charmer on the circuit all season long. We spoke to her at a party for Sony Pictures Classics, the film’s distributor, on Saturday, and she revealed a bit of country pride. “It’s the first time an Australian has been nominated in an Australian film since ‘Shine,'” she said. Her Australian-designed gown had arrived only hours before, and it, too, was a Cinderella moment. “It takes about six able-bodied people to lift me into my frock,” she said. “I’m going to have to lean on my husband walking up the red carpet.” As a first-time nominee, Ms. Weaver had no problem admitting that she really, really wanted to win, and sharing details of her acceptance speech strategy.

headline.main: A Chat With Oscar’s Australian Cinderella

docs.abstract: The flourishing and study of species has been crucial to the survival of humankind. How can we keep them from disappearing?
docs.snippet: The flourishing and study of species has been crucial to the survival of humankind. How can we keep them from disappearing?
docs.lead_paragraph: When adding up the benefits from three centuries of species discoveries, I’m tempted to start, and also stop, with Sir Hans Sloane.  A London physician and naturalist in the 18th century, he collected everything from insects to elephant tusks.  And like a lot of naturalists, he was ridiculed for it, notably by his friend Horace Walpole, who scoffed at Sloane’s fondness for “sharks with one ear, and spiders as big as geese!”   Sloane’s collections would in time give rise to the British Museum, the British Library, and the Natural History Museum, London.  Not a bad legacy for one lifetime.  But it pales beside the result of a collecting trip to Jamaica, on which Sloane also invented milk chocolate.

headline.main: How Species Save Our Lives

docs.abstract: Betty Allen (1927-2009) was respected for both her operatic voice and her leadership at the Harlem School of the Arts.
docs.snippet: Betty Allen (1927-2009) was respected for both her operatic voice and her leadership at the Harlem School of the Arts.
docs.lead_paragraph: The mezzo-soprano Betty Allen was part of a generation of pioneering black female vocal artists who emerged triumphantly in the 1950s and ’60s, a select group of greats including Leontyne Price, Shirley Verrett and Grace Bumbry. If Ms. Allen never achieved the status or the public renown of her sister singers, she was a distinguished performer who combined a rich voice with musical integrity and scrupulous diction; a devotee of American music; and a favorite of composers as varied as Virgil Thomson, Ned Rorem and Leonard Bernstein. As a conductor Bernstein recruited her often to sing with the New York Philharmonic. Yet she may have had her greatest influence as an educator who taught for decades at the Manhattan School of Music and directed the Harlem School of the Arts during 13 high-growth years, becoming its president emeritus in 1993.

docs.lead_paragraph: I hope to be watching the Oscars tonight, at least the red carpet. It starts around 1 a.m. here. Meanwhile, Milan’s obsession with the movies this season persists. The music for Missoni this afternoon came from “True Romance” and “Natural Born Killers,” and the chaotic, pastel clothes brought to mind Juliette Lewis, though not specifically her character in the Oliver Stone film. The mood was girlish innocence verging to girlish wreck, with long silk-print and knit dresses, impressively fat cardigans, and maxi coats in multi-hued python. The colors seem to flood from a girl’s bedroom, or the bathrooms of a 1960s subdivision: baby yellow, mint green, pink, and violet. Angela Missoni threw them together, sometimes causing one to cringe (example: a crinkly violet knit pants outfit with a sick twinkle of Lurex). It was strong and little perverse, thanks to the pastel upchuck. The accessories also pointed to bad movie girls: floppy knit caps and adorable motorcycle boots in a collage of python and colors.

docs.lead_paragraph: Unlike baseball and golf, say, the sport of hockey has not inspired a particularly illustrious body of literature. There are only a handful of decent hockey novels, chief among them “King Leary,” by the Canadian writer Paul Quarrington, and “Amazons,” by one Cleo Birdwell, supposedly the first woman to play in the National Hockey League. “Amazons” is actually by Don DeLillo, but for years now he has disowned the 1980 pseudonymous work, which may indicate something of hockey’s status among American literati, at least. The Liam Neeson thriller “Unknown” (Warner Brothers) sold an estimated $12.4 million for a two-week total of $42.8 million. Adam Sandler’s “Just Go With It” (Sony Pictures Entertainment) was fourth with about $11.1 million, lifting its three-week total to $79.4 million. “I Am Number Four,” a teenage science-fiction thriller from DreamWorks Studios, rounded out the top five with about $11 million for a two-week total of $37.7 million.

docs.abstract: Roman Polanski’s “The Ghost Writer” won a measure of solace on Friday when the French cultural elite showered that thriller with four Césars.
docs.snippet: Roman Polanski’s “The Ghost Writer” won a measure of solace on Friday when the French cultural elite showered that thriller with four Césars.
docs.lead_paragraph: Roman Polanski, whose film “The Ghost Writer” was snubbed by the Oscars, won a measure of solace on Friday when the French cultural elite showered that thriller with four Césars. The honors, France’s version of the Academy Awards, included a best directing nod for Mr. Polanski, who was vigorously supported by French celebrities when he was arrested in 2009 in connection with a 1977 sex charge in the United States and detained in Switzerland until he fended off extradition in July. “I finished this film while in jail, so I would like to thank all the people who helped me and supported me until the very end,” Mr. Polanski said in his speech, referring to his work completing the film while under house arrest. He also shared the César for best adapted screenplay with Robert Harris, while the film also captured awards for best editing and best score. But it was defeated for best picture by “Of Gods and Men,” about French Cistercian Trappist monks slain by Algerian fundamentalists. (That film was spurned by the Oscars in its foreign-language category.) Quentin Tarantino was also celebrated, receiving an honorary career award and a standing ovation.

docs.abstract: There is serious talk among scientists that a new geologic era has begun, called the Anthropocene.
docs.snippet: There is serious talk among scientists that a new geologic era has begun, called the Anthropocene.
docs.lead_paragraph: The edges of historical eras tend to be fuzzy. It would be nice to think that someone awoke in Florence, Italy, one day in the late 1300s  perhaps as spring started and said, “Today the Renaissance begins!” We can be sure no one did, if only because historians discern such eras only in retrospect. The same is true of geological epochs. Humans existed when the Pleistocene ended and the Holocene began, 11,500 years ago. The geologic time scale, which defines geological periods, began to take its modern form only in the 19th century.

docs.abstract: Like most Americans, like most of the planet, I am a sucker for this over-inflated attempt to summarize and recognize the year’s movies.
docs.snippet: Like most Americans, like most of the planet, I am a sucker for this over-inflated attempt to summarize and recognize the year’s movies.
docs.lead_paragraph: My vantage point for the Oscars was a newsroom set for Web television commentary, from which I watched broadcast television. So not the most visibility, but here is what I saw. The Oscars did the job, but then again, they had an awful lot of good movies to work with. At least eight of the movies were worthy of best picture in one way or another, and there were enough twists and turns to keep the show interesting. Can’t say the same about the hosts, who were really a host, namely Anne Hathaway. She gamely soldiered along while James Franco did, um, what exactly? Mr. Franco tweeted about doing the Oscars, made movies about doing the Oscars, gave many interviews about being a host, but when it came time to do the actual Oscars, he entered the witness protection program. Perhaps we should draw some satisfaction from the fact that this time around, it was the man who had the job of standing there and looking pretty. But his frozen smile, punched-out gaze, made you wonder while he was there in the first place.

headline.main: Despite It All, a Night Worth Spending Time With

docs.lead_paragraph: LOS ANGELES— In a year in which younger viewers were aggressively courted, the Oscars rewarded what could be considered the most traditional of traditional Academy bait: a period British drama, set during World War II. The best picture win for “The King’s Speech,” and the corresponding win for Tom Hooper as best director over “The Social Network” and David Fincher, will be fussed over by critics and bloggers as a return to the Academy’s staid tastes. It could equally be called a win for Harvey Weinstein’s aggressive campaigning – an unusually superstitious Mr. Weinstein pulled out every stop short of calling in the Queen to promote his comeback film; oh wait, he did get her seal of approval, along with Rupert Murdoch’s. (His father’s stutter was also cured by Lionel Logue.)

docs.abstract: Though the hosts, James Franco and Anne Hathaway, joked about being the “hip” Oscars from the start of the show, and then acted on it, their performances drew decidedly mixed reviews.
docs.snippet: Though the hosts, James Franco and Anne Hathaway, joked about being the “hip” Oscars from the start of the show, and then acted on it, their performances drew decidedly mixed reviews.
docs.lead_paragraph: LOS ANGELES — So how did the Academy Awards do as a cultural mash-up? Not so hot. Though the hosts, James Franco and Anne Hathaway, joked about being the “hip” Oscars from the start of the show and then acted on it — Mr. Franco unleashed a torrent of backstage Twitter posts, and Ms. Hathaway mentioned drinking games — their performance drew decidedly mixed reviews, especially when compared with the riffing of the 94-year-old Kirk Douglas. The “Auto-Tune the News” segment was a bit of a head-scratcher. And the use of the fifth-grade choir from Staten Island’s P.S. 22, a YouTube sensation known for its renditions of pop and indie songs, was denuded by singing “Somewhere Over the Rainbow” as the credits rolled. Don’t get us wrong, it was still cute (and the shot of Melissa Leo singing along was sweet, especially after she dropped an obscenity in her remarks accepting her Supporting Actress Oscar). But it could have been much sharper. What did you think?

headline.main: A Mixed Bag of a Cultural Mash-Up

docs.lead_paragraph: In today’s puzzles, we have fun tying shoelaces. Most of you have probably spent a significant chunk of time carrying out this mundane activity, maybe a few months of your entire life when it’s all added up. Perhaps it’s even more if you wear lace boots. Done right, shoelaces add to the elegance of footwear. Not done right, they can trip you up or deprive you of an Olympic medal, as might have happened to the notorious ice-skater Tonya Harding in 1994. Nowadays, shoemakers use newfangled ways to make shoes secure, such as velcro fasteners or new space-age materials that need no fasteners at all. To us puzzle lovers, shoelaces provide a wealth of combinatorial delights. So I thought it was worth getting this puzzle out before shoelaces disappear entirely.

docs.abstract: Led by Sara Mearns, City Ballet restored a sense of musicality to dance during its winter season.
docs.snippet: Led by Sara Mearns, City Ballet restored a sense of musicality to dance during its winter season.
docs.lead_paragraph: Though ballet is no better than other forms of dancing, its capacity for large-scale legibility have singular theatrical potency. Its shapes and lines beam far into space. When those geometries meet music, their union occurs not only in the bodies of the dancers: the music seems to animate the air around them. Paradoxically it is often felt more keenly by those in the uppermost rows of the theater than by those seated near the conductor. Ballet can turn music into physics; the connection of time and space becomes full of mysterious significance.

headline.main: At City Ballet This Winter, You Could Sometimes See the Music

docs.abstract: In “Then Everything Changed” Jeff Greenfield turns three what-ifs from the past into a trio of novellas.
docs.snippet: In “Then Everything Changed” Jeff Greenfield turns three what-ifs from the past into a trio of novellas.
docs.lead_paragraph: The “what if?” genre of alternate history has attracted a disparate a crew of practitioners including Newt Gingrich (“1945,” written with William R. Forstchen), Philip Roth (“The Plot Against America”) and Philip K. Dick (“The Man in the High Castle”). It’s yielded best sellers like Robert Harris’s “Fatherland” and literary gems like Michael Chabon’s “Yiddish Policemen’s Union.” And it’s addressed staggering questions like: What if the Nazis won World War II? What if a group of time-traveling white supremacists from South Africa gave Robert E. Lee’s troops AK-47 assault rifles to help the Confederacy win the Civil War?

headline.main: With a Few Tweaks, Shaking Up History
headline.print_headline: With a Few Tweaks, Shaking Up History

docs.snippet: Opposite ABC’s coverage of the Academy Awards on Sunday night rival networks drew mostly meager audiences.
docs.lead_paragraph: Opposite ABC’s coverage of the Academy Awards on Sunday night rival networks drew mostly meager audiences  even as the Oscars, according to Nielsen’s estimates, drew 37.6 million viewers, down from the 41.7 million who watched a year ago. CBS earned second place as it typically has on the night of the award show, garnering modest ratings early in prime time with “60 Minutes” at 7 p.m. (8.4 million) and “The Amazing Race” at 8 (7.6 million). CBS broadcast a repeat of “Undercover Boss” at 9 (5.6 million) followed by “CSI: Miami” at 10 (8.2 million). Fox ranked third with reruns of its animated comedies, including an hourlong repeat of “Family Guy” at 9 (4.3 million). NBC was fourth with “Dateline” at 7 (4.7 million) and a three-hour marathon of “Minute to Win It” reruns, which averaged 2.9 million viewers.

headline.main: Few Winners Against the Oscars

For breakfast.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Even a “small” nuclear war — one involving only 100 Hiroshima-sized bombs — would cause catastrophic global cooling, reduced rainfall and widespread damage to agriculture, a new report by federal scientists finds. [National Geographic]
